subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(1) - Woman Director Mandate
question: Aman Steels Ltd., an unlisted public company, has a paid-up share capital of ₹80 Crores and an annual turnover of ₹320 Crores as per its latest audited financial statements for FY 2023-24. On June 15, 2024, the sole woman director resigned due to personal reasons. What is the statutory time limit by which the company must fill the intermittent vacancy under Section 149(1) read with Rule 3 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014?
options: At the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of vacancy, whichever is later.
Within 30 days from the date of resignation submitted by the woman director.
Within 6 months from the date of vacancy as per the General Circular of MCA.
At the immediate next Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the company.
ref: Section 149(1) second proviso read with Rule 3 of Companies (Appointment & Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 149(1) and Rule 3, every listed company and every unlisted public company having paid-up share capital ≥ ₹100 Crore OR turnover ≥ ₹300 Crore must have at least one woman director. Since turnover is ₹320 Cr, the rule applies. Any intermittent vacancy must be filled by the Board at the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of such vacancy, whichever is later.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(4) & 149(6) - Independent Director Qualification & Tenure
question: Mr. Rajan was appointed as an Independent Director of Trident Pharma Ltd. for a term of 5 consecutive years commencing April 1, 2019. In July 2023, his son was appointed as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a subsidiary company of Trident Pharma Ltd. Trident Pharma Ltd. now proposes to re-appoint Mr. Rajan for a second consecutive term of 5 years with effect from April 1, 2024. Which of the following statements is legally correct under Section 149(6)?
options: Mr. Rajan is disqualified from being appointed as an Independent Director because his relative (son) holds the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (CFO) in a subsidiary company during the preceding three financial years.
Mr. Rajan can be re-appointed by passing an Ordinary Resolution in general meeting without any impediment since the son is in a subsidiary, not the holding company.
Mr. Rajan can only be appointed if approval from the Central Government (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) is obtained prior to general meeting.
The restriction on relatives being KMP applies only to spouse and parents, not sons or daughters under the definition of relative in Section 2(77).
ref: Section 149(6)(e)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 149(6)(e)(i), a person is not eligible to be an Independent Director if none of his relatives holds or has held the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) or is or has been employee of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company in any of the three financial years immediately preceding the financial year in which he is proposed to be appointed. Since the son is a KMP (CFO) in a subsidiary, Mr. Rajan ceases to meet the independence criteria.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 164(2) - Disqualification of Directors for Company Default
question: Apex Motors Ltd. failed to file its financial statements and annual returns for three continuous financial years (FY 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23) with the Registrar of Companies. Mr. Vikram was appointed as an additional director on the Board of Apex Motors Ltd. on December 1, 2023. On January 10, 2024, another company, Zenith Infotech Ltd., where Mr. Vikram was already a director, intends to re-appoint him at its AGM. Under Section 164(2) proviso, what is the status of Mr. Vikram's disqualification?
options: Mr. Vikram shall not incur disqualification under Section 164(2) in Zenith Infotech Ltd. for a period of six months from the date of his appointment in Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram incurs immediate automatic disqualification under Section 164(2) for 5 years across all companies from the moment he joined Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram is disqualified for lifetime from being appointed as director in any public company unless compounded by NCLT.
Disqualification under Section 164(2) applies only to Managing Directors and Whole-Time Directors, exempting Additional Directors.
ref: Section 164(2) proviso (inserted by Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017)
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 164(2), where a person is appointed as a director of a company which is in default of clause (a) or clause (b) of subsection (2), he shall not incur the disqualification for a period of six months from the date of his appointment. This provides a 6-month grace period for newly appointed directors to rectify defaults.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 165 - Maximum Number of Directorships
question: Ms. Shalini currently holds directorships in 18 companies, comprising 8 public companies and 10 private companies. Two of the private companies are dormant companies under Section 455, and one is a Section 8 non-profit company. She is now offered an alternate directorship in an unlisted public company. Can Ms. Shalini accept this new directorship without violating Section 165?
options: Yes, because dormant companies and Section 8 companies are excluded from the ceiling of 20 total companies and 10 public companies under Section 165, and alternate directorship is counted towards the ceiling.
No, because alternate directorships cannot be counted under any circumstances under the Companies Act, 2013.
No, because a person can never hold directorship in more than 10 companies of any class under the revised MCA norms.
Yes, but only if prior approval of the Central Government is obtained through Form DIR-12.
ref: Section 165(1) read with Explanation I & II of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 165(1), the maximum number of directorships is 20, of which public companies cannot exceed 10. Directorship in a dormant company (Sec 455) and Section 8 company are excluded from the limit. Alternate directorship is explicitly included in calculating limits. Here: Active public companies = 8 (+1 proposed = 9 ≤ 10); Active total = 8 public + 8 active private = 16 (+1 = 17 ≤ 20). Hence, she can legally accept.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 173 - Board Meetings & Quorum for Interested Directors
question: The Board of Directors of Pioneer Infrastructure Ltd. consists of 9 directors. At a meeting convened to consider a commercial contract involving an entity in which 7 directors are interested under Section 184(2), only 2 non-interested directors are present in person. What constitutes a valid quorum for transacting this specific business under Section 174(3)?
options: The quorum shall be the number of non-interested directors who are present at the meeting being not less than two.
A minimum of one-third of the total strength (i.e., 3 directors) is mandatory; hence the meeting must be adjourned for want of quorum.
All 7 interested directors can vote after making an oral disclosure of interest in the meeting.
The contract must be referred directly to the Central Government since quorum cannot be formed.
ref: Section 174(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 174(3), where at any time the number of interested directors exceeds or is equal to two-thirds of the total strength of the Board, the number of directors who are not interested and present at the meeting, being not less than two, shall be the quorum during such time for that business. Here 7 out of 9 are interested (≥ 2/3rd = 6); the 2 disinterested directors present constitute valid quorum.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 177 - Audit Committee Mandatory Constitution & Functions
question: Kiran Fabricators Ltd., an unlisted public company, has paid-up share capital of ₹8 Crores, turnover of ₹85 Crores, and outstanding bank borrowings and debentures aggregating ₹120 Crores. Is the company required to constitute an Audit Committee under Section 177 read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because its outstanding loans, borrowings, debentures or deposits exceed ₹50 Crores.
No, because paid-up capital is below ₹10 Crores and turnover is below ₹100 Crores.
No, constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory only for equity-listed public companies.
Yes, but only if at least 100 members requisition the Board in writing.
ref: Section 177(1) read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board & Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 4, the Board of every unlisted public company having: (a) paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 Cr; OR (b) turnover ≥ ₹100 Cr; OR (c) outstanding loans, debentures, deposits > ₹50 Cr, must constitute an Audit Committee. Since borrowings/debentures are ₹120 Cr (> ₹50 Cr), constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 185 - Loans to Directors & Controlled Entities
question: Solaris Power Ltd. desires to advance a loan of ₹15 Crores to Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Mr. Arvind is a director of Solaris Power Ltd. and holds 28% of the total voting power in Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Under the amended Section 185, under what conditions can Solaris Power Ltd. advance this loan?
options: A special resolution must be passed in general meeting with explanatory statement disclosing full particulars, and the borrowing company must utilise the loan exclusively for its principal business activities.
The loan is completely prohibited under Section 185(1) as loans to any entity where a director holds >20% voting power cannot be given under any circumstances.
Only an ordinary resolution in Board meeting is required with the consent of all directors present.
The loan can be given only with prior approval of NCLT and Reserve Bank of India.
ref: Section 185(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 185(2), a company may advance any loan or give guarantee/security to any person in whom any of the directors is interested (which includes a private company where a director holds ≥25% voting power) provided: (a) a special resolution is passed in general meeting; and (b) the loans are utilised by the borrowing company for its principal business activities.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 186 - Loans & Investments by Company
question: Blue Horizon Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹50 Crores, free reserves of ₹30 Crores, and securities premium account of ₹20 Crores. The Board of Directors wishes to grant a loan of ₹65 Crores to a business partner firm. What is the statutory requirement under Section 186(3) for giving this loan?
options: Prior approval by Special Resolution in general meeting is mandatory, because the aggregate loan exceeds 60% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium (60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr) and 100% of free reserves & securities premium (₹50 Cr).
Only unanimous Board resolution is sufficient as the amount is less than 100% of paid-up capital.
Ordinary resolution in AGM is sufficient with prior sanction of ROC.
No resolution is needed if the rate of interest is higher than the bank rate.
ref: Section 186(2) and 186(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 186(2), a company cannot directly or indirectly give loan/guarantee/security exceeding 60% of (Paid-up capital + Free reserves + Securities premium) OR 100% of (Free reserves + Securities premium), whichever is more, without prior approval by special resolution. Here: 60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr; 100% of ₹50 Cr = ₹50 Cr. Threshold = ₹60 Cr. Since proposed loan is ₹65 Cr (> ₹60 Cr), prior Special Resolution is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 188 - Related Party Transactions & Threshold Limits
question: Sigma Electronics Ltd., a public company, proposes to enter into a contract for sale of manufactured goods amounting to ₹120 Crores to Delta Components Pvt. Ltd., an entity where the Managing Director of Sigma holds 30% shares. The annual turnover of Sigma Electronics Ltd. as per its latest audited balance sheet is ₹900 Crores. Does this transaction require prior approval by Ordinary Resolution under Section 188 read with Rule 15?
options: Yes, because the contract value of ₹120 Crores exceeds 10% of the annual turnover of the company (10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr).
No, approval of shareholders is needed only if contract value exceeds ₹100 Crores regardless of turnover.
No, only Audit Committee approval is needed; shareholder resolution is never required for sale of goods.
Yes, but it requires a Special Resolution passed with 75% majority, not an Ordinary Resolution.
ref: Section 188(1) read with Rule 15(3) of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 15(3)(a)(i), contracts or arrangements with respect to sale, purchase or supply of any goods or materials directly or through appointment of agent exceeding 10% of turnover requires prior approval of the company by ordinary resolution. 10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr. Since ₹120 Cr > ₹90 Cr, prior ordinary resolution in general meeting is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 197 & Schedule V - Managerial Remuneration Limits
question: Quantum Infotech Ltd., a public company with 3 whole-time directors and 1 managing director, has earned a net profit of ₹40 Crores computed under Section 198 for FY 2023-24. What is the maximum managerial remuneration payable to all managerial personnel without seeking approval of the Central Government?
options: 10% of net profits (₹4.0 Crores) if there is more than one such director, and overall 11% of net profits (₹4.4 Crores) for all directors including non-executive directors.
5% of net profits regardless of the number of whole-time directors.
15% of net profits provided unanimous consent of the Board of Directors is obtained.
Unlimited remuneration provided an ordinary resolution is passed in the Annual General Meeting.
ref: Section 197(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 197(1), total managerial remuneration payable by a public company to its directors shall not exceed 11% of net profits. Remuneration payable to any one managing director or whole-time director shall not exceed 5% of net profits, and if there is more than one such director, remuneration shall not exceed 10% of net profits to all of them together. Beyond 11%, a special resolution is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 203 - Mandatory Appointment of KMP
question: Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has a paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores and turnover of ₹80 Crores. Is Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. mandatorily required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary under Section 203 read with Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because every private company having a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more is required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary.
No, mandatory appointment of KMP applies exclusively to listed public companies.
No, the threshold for private companies was raised to ₹50 Crores in the recent MCA amendment.
Yes, but only if the company has more than 200 employees on its payroll.
ref: Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 8A (as amended w.e.f. April 1, 2020), every private company which has a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more shall have a whole-time company secretary. Since Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores (≥ ₹10 Cr), it must appoint a whole-time CS.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 101 & 103 - Notice of General Meeting & Quorum
question: A public company having 4,500 members convenes an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM). At the appointed time, only 12 members are personally present. After waiting for 30 minutes, 14 members are personally present. What is the legal consequence regarding quorum under Section 103?
options: The meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, because the required quorum for a company having between 1,000 and 5,000 members is 15 members personally present.
The 14 members present constitute valid quorum since the shortfall is less than 10%.
The meeting is immediately dissolved as an EGM cannot be adjourned under any circumstances.
The Chairman can use his casting vote to declare quorum validly established.
ref: Section 103(1)(a) and 103(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 103(1)(a), for a public company: (i) 5 members personally present if members ≤ 1,000; (ii) 15 members if members > 1,000 but ≤ 5,000; (iii) 30 members if members > 5,000. Here members = 4,500, so quorum is 15 members personally present. Since only 14 were present within 30 minutes, the meeting stands adjourned to next week unless called by requisitionists.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 135 - Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Expenditure
question: Avon Chemicals Ltd. had an unspent CSR amount of ₹45 Lakhs relating to an 'ongoing project' for FY 2023-24. By what date must this unspent amount be transferred to a special account, and within what period must it be spent under Section 135(6)?
options: Transferred to 'Unspent CSR Account' in a scheduled bank within 30 days from the end of the financial year, and spent within 3 financial years from the date of transfer.
Transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 6 months from the end of the financial year.
Carried forward in general reserves indefinitely with approval of the Board of Directors.
Refunded to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs within 90 days from the Annual General Meeting.
ref: Section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 135(6), any unspent CSR amount pursuant to any ongoing project shall be transferred by the company within 30 days from the end of the financial year to a special account titled 'Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account', and such amount shall be spent within a period of 3 financial years from the date of such transfer, failing which it must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days from completion of the third financial year.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 168 - Resignation of Director & Effective Date
question: Dr. Nair, an independent director of Bharat Biotech Ltd., tendered his resignation via a written notice dated October 5, specifying that the resignation shall take effect from November 1. The company received the notice on October 8, and the Board noted the resignation on October 20. Under Section 168(2), what is the effective date of Dr. Nair's resignation?
options: November 1, because the resignation takes effect from the date specified in the notice since it is later than the date of receipt.
October 5, the date on which the letter was drafted and signed.
October 8, the date on which the company received the notice.
October 20, the date on which the Board took formal record of the resignation.
ref: Section 168(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 168(2), the resignation of a director shall take effect from the date on which the notice is received by the company or the date, if any, specified by the director in the notice, whichever is later. Here specified date (Nov 1) is later than receipt date (Oct 8); hence effective date is November 1.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 180 - Restrictions on Powers of Board
question: The Board of Directors of Pioneer Logistics Ltd. intends to sell an undertaking comprising a specialized fleet division whose book value is ₹42 Crores. The company's total net worth as per the audited balance sheet of the preceding financial year is ₹180 Crores. Does this sale require authorization by Special Resolution under Section 180(1)(a)?
options: Yes, because the investment in the undertaking exceeds 20% of the net worth of the company (20% of ₹180 Cr = ₹36 Cr).
No, because Board approval alone is sufficient for selling assets unless the whole company is being liquidated.
No, ordinary resolution in general meeting is sufficient under the amended rules.
Yes, but only if financial institutions have a charge registered over the undertaking.
ref: Section 180(1)(a) read with Explanation (i) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 180(1)(a), the Board can sell, lease or dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of the undertaking only with the consent of the company by special resolution. An 'undertaking' means an undertaking in which the investment of the company exceeds 20% of its net worth OR which generates 20% of total income. Here ₹42 Cr / ₹180 Cr = 23.33% (> 20%). Hence Special Resolution is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 184 - Disclosure of Interest by Directors
question: Mr. Somani, a director of Nexus Tech Ltd., enters into a contract on behalf of Nexus Tech Ltd. with a partnership firm in which his wife holds a 60% share. Mr. Somani does not disclose his interest at the Board meeting where the contract is discussed and voted on. What are the legal consequences under Section 184(4) and Section 184(3)?
options: The contract shall be voidable at the option of Nexus Tech Ltd., and Mr. Somani shall be punishable with fine which may extend to ₹1,00,000, and shall vacate office under Section 167(1)(c).
The contract is valid and binding provided it is executed at fair arm's length market price.
Mr. Somani is solely subjected to a reprimand by the Chairman without any statutory penalty.
The firm must be compulsorily converted into a private limited company within 3 months.
ref: Section 184(3) and 184(4) read with Section 167(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 184(3), a contract entered into by the company without disclosure of interest under subsection (2) shall be voidable at the option of the company. Under Section 184(4), non-compliance attracts fine up to ₹1,00,000. Under Section 167(1)(c), the director shall vacate his office if he fails to disclose his interest.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 110 - Passing of Resolutions by Postal Ballot
question: Greenfield Agro Ltd., an unlisted public company with 800 members, wishes to pass an ordinary resolution for the alteration of the objects clause of its Memorandum of Association. Which of the following modes is legally mandated or permissible under Section 110 read with Rule 22?
options: Alteration of objects clause for which money was raised from public through prospectus requires passing resolution only by postal ballot, but companies having members up to 200 are exempt from postal ballot rules.
Postal ballot is optional and the resolution can only be transacted at an Annual General Meeting.
Postal ballot can never be used for changing the objects clause under the Companies Act, 2013.
Postal ballot requires physical ballot papers only; electronic voting is prohibited for alteration of objects.
ref: Section 110(1) read with Rule 22 of Companies (Management & Administration) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Section 110(1) read with Rule 22(16), alteration of objects clause of MOA is an item of business which must be transacted only by means of postal ballot (which includes electronic voting). However, One Person Companies and companies having members up to 200 are not required to transact any business through postal ballot.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 161(2) - Appointment of Alternate Director
question: Mr. Adams, a non-executive director of Horizon Global Ltd., goes abroad for a continuous period of 5 months. The Board appoints Mr. Verma as an alternate director. Mr. Verma is already an alternate director for another director in the same company. Can Mr. Verma act as an alternate director for Mr. Adams under Section 161(2)?
options: No, because a person cannot be appointed as an alternate director for more than one director in the same company, nor if he holds any directorship in the same company.
Yes, a person can hold up to three alternate directorships in the same company.
Yes, provided approval of shareholders by special resolution is obtained within 30 days.
No, because an alternate director can only be appointed if the original director is absent for at least 12 months.
ref: Section 161(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 161(2), the Board of Directors of a company may appoint a person, not being a person holding any alternate directorship for any other director in the company or holding directorship in the same company, to act as an alternate director for a director during his absence for a period of not less than 3 months from India. Hence, Mr. Verma cannot be appointed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 167 - Vacation of Office of Director
question: Mr. Kapoor, director of Sterling Castings Ltd., fails to attend any Board meetings held during a period of 12 continuous months, even though leave of absence was granted to him for all meetings. Under Section 167(1)(b), what is the legal position of Mr. Kapoor's directorship?
options: His office as director becomes vacant automatically from the date of the meeting held immediately after the expiry of 12 months, regardless of whether leave of absence was granted or not.
His office remains intact because leave of absence was formally granted by the Board.
Vacation takes effect only after the company sends a 30-day show cause notice to Mr. Kapoor.
Vacation applies only if he misses 6 consecutive general meetings of shareholders.
ref: Section 167(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 167(1)(b), the office of a director shall become vacant in case he absents himself from all the meetings of the Board of Directors held during a period of twelve months with or without seeking leave of absence of the Board. Thus, obtaining leave of absence does not protect a director if he is absent for 12 continuous months.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 178 - Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC)
question: Starlight Textiles Ltd., an unlisted public company, has paid-up share capital of ₹15 Crores, turnover of ₹80 Crores, and bank loans of ₹40 Crores. Does Starlight Textiles Ltd. require the constitution of a Nomination and Remuneration Committee under Section 178(1) read with Rule 6?
options: Yes, because its paid-up share capital exceeds ₹10 Crores.
No, because its turnover is below ₹100 Crores and borrowings are below ₹50 Crores.
No, NRC is required only for listed entities with market capitalization > ₹1,000 Crores.
Yes, but only if it employs more than 500 contract workers.
ref: Section 178(1) read with Rule 6 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Section 178(1) read with Rule 6, every listed public company and unlisted public companies having: (a) paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 Cr; OR (b) turnover ≥ ₹100 Cr; OR (c) outstanding loans/debentures/deposits > ₹50 Cr, must constitute a Nomination and Remuneration Committee. Since paid-up capital is ₹15 Cr (≥ ₹10 Cr), NRC is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 271 - Grounds for Winding Up by Tribunal
question: Under Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013 (as amended by IBC 2016), which of the following is NOT a permissible ground for the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to order the winding up of a company?
options: Inability of the company to pay its debts upon receipt of a statutory demand notice from an operational creditor.
The company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, or public order.
The Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.
The company has made a default in filing with the Registrar its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years.
ref: Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Schedule XI)
explanation: Under Section 271 as amended by IBC 2016, 'inability to pay debts' was deleted from Section 271 and shifted exclusively to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (CIRP). The remaining grounds under Sec 271 are: special resolution, acting against sovereignty/integrity of India, fraudulent conduct (Sec 213), default in filing financial statements/annual returns for 5 consecutive years, and just and equitable ground.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 272 - Petitioners for Winding Up
question: A petition for winding up of Mayur Finlease Ltd. is presented before the NCLT by the Registrar of Companies on the ground that the company has defaulted in filing its financial statements for 5 consecutive financial years. Under Section 272(3), what condition precedent must be satisfied by the Registrar before presenting this petition?
options: The Registrar must obtain previous sanction of the Central Government, and the Central Government shall not accord sanction without giving the company a reasonable opportunity of making representations.
The Registrar must obtain approval of at least 75% of the secured creditors of the company.
The Registrar must publish a notice in the Official Gazette at least 90 days before filing.
No sanction is required if default exceeds 3 years.
ref: Section 272(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 272(3), the Registrar shall not present a petition on any grounds specified in subsection (1) except on the ground specified in clause (b) or (d) or (e) of Section 271, and only after obtaining the previous sanction of the Central Government. The Central Government shall not accord sanction without giving the company a reasonable opportunity of making representations.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 281 - Submission of Report by Company Liquidator
question: The NCLT passes a winding up order appointing Mr. Deshmukh as the Company Liquidator of Falcon Engineering Ltd. Under Section 281(1), within what timeframe from the date of the winding up order must the Company Liquidator submit a preliminary report to the Tribunal?
options: Within 60 days from the date of the winding up order.
Within 30 days from the date of his appointment.
Within 180 days from the date of admission of the petition.
Within 1 year from the date of receipt of the statement of affairs.
ref: Section 281(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 281(1), where the Tribunal has made a winding up order or appointed a Company Liquidator, such liquidator shall, within 60 days from the date of the order, submit to the Tribunal a report containing particulars of assets, cash, debts, liabilities, and failure causes.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 326 & 327 - Overriding Preferential Payments (Workmen Dues)
question: In the winding up of Premier Textiles Ltd., the assets realize ₹10 Crores. The claims comprise: (a) Workmen's dues for the period of 24 months preceding the winding up order: ₹4 Crores; (b) Debt due to secured creditors having pari passu charge: ₹8 Crores; (c) Statutory taxes to Central Govt: ₹2 Crores. Under Section 326, how shall the realized proceeds of ₹10 Crores be distributed between workmen's dues and secured creditors?
options: Pari passu in proportion to their respective claims (Workmen get ₹3.33 Crores and Secured Creditors get ₹6.67 Crores) as overriding preferential payments, leaving zero for taxes.
Secured creditors are paid in full ₹8 Crores first, and remaining ₹2 Crores is paid to workmen.
Workmen dues of ₹4 Crores are paid in full first, and remaining ₹6 Crores is paid to secured creditors.
Statutory taxes of ₹2 Crores have first sovereign charge, and balance ₹8 Crores is shared equally.
ref: Section 326(1) and 326(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 326(1) (Overriding Preferential Payments), workmen's dues and debts due to secured creditors to the extent of the workmen's portion shall be paid in priority to all other debts. If the assets are insufficient to meet them in full, they shall abate in equal proportions (pari passu). Ratio of workmen (₹4 Cr) : secured debt (₹8 Cr) = 1:2. Out of ₹10 Cr: Workmen receive ₹3.33 Cr and Secured Creditors receive ₹6.67 Cr.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 328 - Fraudulent Preference in Winding Up
question: Omega Steels Ltd. made a transfer of property to an unsecured creditor, Mr. Bansal, to clear an antecedent loan on February 10, 2024. A petition for winding up was presented before NCLT on July 15, 2024, and winding up was ordered. The Company Liquidator applies under Section 328 to declare the transaction invalid. What is the look-back period for fraudulent preference under Section 328?
options: Any transfer made within 6 months before the presentation of the petition for winding up, if made with a view to give preference over other creditors.
Any transfer made within 1 year before the date of the winding up order.
Any transfer made within 2 years before insolvency initiation in case of related parties.
Any transaction made within 30 days prior to appointment of Provisional Liquidator.
ref: Section 328 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 328(1), where a company has given preference to any person who is a creditor or a surety or a guarantor, and the company does anything which has the effect of putting that person in a position better than other creditors in winding up, and such transaction took place within a period of six months before the presentation of a petition for winding up, it shall be deemed a fraudulent preference and invalid.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 420 & 421 - Appeal to NCLAT & Limitation Period
question: The NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order against Crystal Glass Ltd. on May 10, 2024. The certified copy was received by Crystal Glass Ltd. on May 15, 2024. By what date must Crystal Glass Ltd. file an appeal before the NCLAT under Section 421(3), and what is the maximum condonable delay under the proviso?
options: File within 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order is made available (i.e. by June 29, 2024), with NCLAT having power to condone delay up to a further period not exceeding 45 days.
File within 30 days, with condonable delay of 15 days.
File within 60 days, with no power of condonation for delay.
File within 90 days from the date of pronouncement of the order.
ref: Section 421(3) and Section 421(4) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 421(3), every appeal to NCLAT shall be filed within a period of 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order of the Tribunal is made available to the person aggrieved. Under Section 421(4), NCLAT may entertain an appeal after 45 days if satisfied there was sufficient cause, for a further period not exceeding 45 days.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 423 - Appeal to Supreme Court
question: Any person aggrieved by any order of the Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) may file an appeal to the Supreme Court of India under Section 423 of the Companies Act, 2013. On what grounds can such appeal be filed, and within what timeframe?
options: On any question of law arising out of such order, within 60 days from the date of receipt of the order, with power to condone delay up to a further 60 days.
On any question of fact or law, within 30 days from the date of the order without any extension.
Only on violation of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 within 90 days.
Only on criminal contempt findings within 45 days.
ref: Section 423 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 423, any person aggrieved by any order of the Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court of India on any question of law arising out of such order within 60 days from the date of communication of the order. The Supreme Court may condone delay for a further period not exceeding 60 days.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 430 - Civil Court Bar of Jurisdiction
question: A shareholder of Marvel Estates Ltd. files a civil suit in the City Civil Court seeking an injunction against the company from holding an Extraordinary General Meeting. The company argues that the Civil Court has no jurisdiction. Under Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the legal position?
options: No civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the NCLT or NCLAT is empowered to determine by or under this Act, and no injunction shall be granted by any court.
Civil courts have concurrent jurisdiction with NCLT in all shareholder dispute matters.
Civil courts can issue temporary injunctions up to 30 days before transferring the case to NCLT.
Section 430 applies only to winding up matters, leaving general meeting issues to High Courts.
ref: Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 430, no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force, and no injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by this Act.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 273 - Powers of Tribunal on Petition
question: Upon hearing a winding up petition under Section 273, the NCLT decides that an order of winding up would unfairly prejudice the petitioners, but that otherwise the facts justify winding up under the just and equitable ground. What order can the Tribunal pass under Section 273(1)?
options: The Tribunal may refuse to make an order of winding up and make any other interim or final order as it thinks fit, including orders under Chapter XVI (Oppression and Mismanagement).
The Tribunal is bound to pass an immediate winding up order regardless of unfair prejudice.
The Tribunal must refer the company compulsorily to the Central Government for nationalization.
The Tribunal must dismiss the petition with exemplary costs on the petitioners.
ref: Section 273(1) and 273(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 273(2), where the petition is presented on the ground that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up, the Tribunal may refuse to make an order of winding up if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking to have the company wound up instead of pursuing that other remedy.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 277 - Intimation to Company Liquidator & ROC
question: When a winding up order is passed by the Tribunal under Section 277, within what period must the Registrar of the Tribunal send intimation to the Company Liquidator and the Registrar of Companies?
options: Within a period not exceeding 7 days from the date of the order.
Within 24 hours of pronouncement.
Within 30 days of drawing up the certified decree.
Within 14 days from the date the order is signed by the President of NCLT.
ref: Section 277(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 277(1), where the Tribunal makes an order for appointment of provisional liquidator or for winding up of a company, it shall, within a period not exceeding seven days from the date of passing of the order, cause intimation thereof to be sent to the Company Liquidator or provisional liquidator and to the Registrar of Companies.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 282 - Advisory Committee in Winding Up
question: Under Section 282 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal may direct that an Advisory Committee be constituted to advise the Company Liquidator. What is the maximum number of members in such an Advisory Committee?
options: Not more than 12 members being creditors and contributories of the company.
Exactly 5 members appointed by the Central Government.
Not more than 20 members representing employees and trade unions.
Any number decided by the Company Liquidator without ceiling.
ref: Section 282(1) and 282(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 282(2), the Advisory Committee shall consist of not more than twelve members, being creditors and contributories of the company or persons holding general or special powers of attorney from creditors or contributories, in such proportions as the Tribunal may direct.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 336 - Offences by Officers in Winding Up
question: Mr. Saxena, a former managing director of an entity under winding up, fails without reasonable excuse to deliver to the Company Liquidator all books and papers of the company within his custody. Under Section 336(1)(b), what punishment is prescribed?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 3 years but which may extend to 5 years and fine from ₹1 Lakh to ₹3 Lakhs.
Simple warning and fine up to ₹10,000.
Suspension of voting rights in general meeting for 1 year.
Civil liability to pay interest at 18% per annum on unrecovered assets.
ref: Section 336(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 336(1), if any past or present officer of a company being wound up fails to deliver up to the Company Liquidator all books and papers belonging to the company, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to five years and with fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to three lakh rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 424 - Procedure Before NCLT & Principles of Natural Justice
question: Under Section 424(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, is the National Company Law Tribunal bound by the rules laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC)?
options: No, the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid down in CPC 1908, but shall be guided by the principles of natural justice and have power to regulate their own procedure.
Yes, the Tribunal must strictly follow every Order and Rule of CPC 1908 without deviation.
The Tribunal is bound by the Indian Penal Code and Evidence Act, but exempt from CPC.
The Tribunal is bound only by High Court original side rules.
ref: Section 424(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 424(1), the Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but shall be guided by the principles of natural justice and, subject to the other provisions of this Act and of any rules made by the Central Government, the Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal shall have power to regulate their own procedure.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 425 - Power of NCLT to Punish for Contempt
question: What powers does the National Company Law Tribunal have with respect to punishing individuals or entities for contempt of its own orders under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013?
options: The Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal shall have the same jurisdiction, powers and authority in respect of contempt of themselves as the High Court has under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
NCLT cannot punish for contempt; it must file a reference before the respective High Court.
NCLT can only impose monetary fines up to ₹500 without power of civil imprisonment.
Contempt powers are vested exclusively in the Ministry of Law and Justice.
ref: Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 425, the Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal shall have the same jurisdiction, powers and authority in respect of contempt of themselves as the High Court has and may exercise, for this purpose, the powers under the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 279 - Stay of Suits on Winding Up Order
question: Once a winding up order has been made by the NCLT or a provisional liquidator has been appointed, what is the effect on existing legal suits and proceedings against the company under Section 279?
options: No suit or other legal proceeding shall be commenced, or if pending at the date of the winding up order, shall be proceeded with, by or against the company, except with the leave of the Tribunal.
All pending civil suits automatically terminate without any right of revival.
Criminal proceedings against directors are stayed permanently.
Secured creditors lose all rights to enforce charges outside the Tribunal.
ref: Section 279(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 279(1), when a winding up order has been passed or a provisional liquidator has been appointed, no suit or other legal proceeding shall be commenced, or if pending at the date of the winding up order, shall be proceeded with, by or against the company, except with the leave of the Tribunal and subject to such terms as the Tribunal may impose.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 327 - Preferential Payments Ranking
question: Under Section 327 of the Companies Act, 2013, in what priority are the debts paid subject to the overriding provisions of Section 326?
options: Revenues, taxes, cesses and rates due to Central/State Govt or local authority accrued within 12 months next before relevant date, followed by wages/salaries of employees for not exceeding 4 months.
Unsecured trade creditors are paid before governmental taxes.
Debenture holders with floating charge are paid after ordinary trade suppliers.
Equity shareholders are paid before statutory provident fund dues.
ref: Section 327(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 327(1), subject to Section 326, in a winding up there shall be paid in priority to all other debts: (a) all revenues, taxes, cesses and rates due from the company to the Central Government or a State Government or to a local authority at the relevant date and having become due and payable within twelve months next before that date; (b) all wages or salary of employees not exceeding 4 months.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 332 - Effect of Floating Charge in Winding Up
question: Zenith Mills Ltd. created a floating charge on its undertaking on January 1, 2024, to secure an existing unsecured debt of ₹50 Lakhs without any fresh cash injection. The company went into winding up on May 15, 2024 (within 12 months). Under Section 332, what is the validity of this floating charge?
options: The floating charge is completely invalid unless it is proved that the company immediately after the creation of the charge was solvent.
The floating charge remains 100% valid since it was registered with ROC within 30 days.
The floating charge converts automatically into an equitable mortgage.
The charge is valid only up to 50% of the loan value.
ref: Section 332 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 332, where a company is being wound up, a floating charge on the undertaking or property of the company created within twelve months immediately preceding the commencement of the winding up shall, unless it is proved that the company immediately after the creation of the charge was solvent, be invalid, except to the amount of any cash paid to the company at the time of or subsequently to the creation of the charge.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 302 & 365 - Dissolution of Company by Tribunal
question: When the affairs of a company have been completely wound up, what is the final statutory step taken by the Company Liquidator under Section 365?
options: The Company Liquidator applies to the Tribunal for an order of dissolution, and the Tribunal shall make an order that the company be dissolved from the date of the order, which the liquidator forwards to ROC within 30 days.
The Company Liquidator simply cancels the PAN card of the company without any court order.
The shareholders pass an unanimous resolution in general meeting to extinguish company name.
The Registrar of Companies issues a striking-off notice under Section 248.
ref: Section 365 of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 365(1), when the affairs of a company have been completely wound up, the Company Liquidator shall make an application to the Tribunal for the dissolution of the company. The Tribunal shall make an order that the company be dissolved from the date of the order. The liquidator must file a copy of the order with ROC within 30 days.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 435 - Establishment of Special Courts
question: For the speedy trial of offences punishable under the Companies Act, 2013 with imprisonment of two years or more, who establishes Special Courts under Section 435?
options: The Central Government, by notification, establishing Special Courts consisting of a single judge holding office as Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge.
The Chief Justice of the High Court on petition of the Registrar of Companies.
The President of the National Company Law Tribunal.
The Bar Council of India in consultation with ICAI.
ref: Section 435(1) and 435(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 435(1), the Central Government may, for the purpose of providing speedy trial of offences punishable under this Act with imprisonment of two years or more, establish Special Courts. A Special Court shall consist of a single judge who shall be appointed by the Central Government with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 441 - Compounding of Certain Offences
question: Under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following offences CANNOT be compounded by the Regional Director or NCLT?
options: Any offence punishable with imprisonment only, or with imprisonment and also with fine.
Any technical offence punishable with fine only up to ₹25 Lakhs.
Any offence of failure to file annual returns with ROC.
Any offence relating to non-maintenance of registered office.
ref: Section 441(1) and 441(6) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 441(6), any offence which is punishable under this Act with imprisonment only, or with imprisonment and also with fine, cannot be compounded. Only offences punishable with fine only, or with imprisonment or fine or with both, can be compounded under Section 441.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 7 - Designated Partners Requirement & Residency
question: Apex Advisors LLP has 4 partners: Two are individuals (one an Indian citizen residing in Dubai who stayed in India for 80 days in FY 2023-24, and one a French national residing in India for 195 days in FY 2023-24), and two are body corporates. Who can be appointed as Designated Partners under Section 7 of the LLP Act, 2008 (as amended)?
options: Every LLP must have at least two designated partners who are individuals and at least one of them shall be a resident in India (stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year); the French national qualifies as resident in India.
Only Indian citizens can be appointed as designated partners; foreign nationals are strictly barred.
Designated partners can only be corporate entities through their managing directors.
Residency requires a minimum stay of 182 days during the immediately preceding seven years.
ref: Section 7(1) of LLP Act 2008 read with amended Explanation by LLP (Amendment) Act 2021
explanation: Under Section 7(1), every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals and at least one of them shall be a resident in India. Under the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021, 'resident in India' means a person who has stayed in India for a period of not less than 120 days during the financial year. Citizenship is not required. Since the French national stayed 195 days (≥ 120 days), he satisfies the residency requirement.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 26 & 27 - Extent of Liability of LLP & Partner as Agent
question: Mr. Dave, a partner in Zenith Logistics LLP, entered into a supply contract with a vendor for ₹25 Lakhs in the ordinary course of the business of the LLP. However, under the internal registered LLP Agreement, partners' borrowing/contracting power was capped at ₹10 Lakhs without prior approval of all partners. The vendor was unaware of this internal restriction. Is the LLP bound by the contract under Section 27?
options: Yes, the LLP is liable because a partner is an agent of the LLP, and the LLP is bound unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that he had no authority or did not believe him to be a partner.
No, the contract is ultra vires the LLP Agreement and completely void ab initio.
Mr. Dave alone is personally liable for the full ₹25 Lakhs, and the LLP is completely exempt.
The contract is enforceable only up to ₹10 Lakhs, and balance ₹15 Lakhs is unenforceable.
ref: Section 27(1) and 27(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 27(2), an LLP is liable for an obligation arising from a contract or otherwise in the course of its business. Under Section 27(1), an LLP is not bound by anything done by a partner in dealing with a person if: (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP; AND (b) the person knows that he has no authority or does not know or believe him to be a partner. Since the vendor had no knowledge of the internal limit, the LLP is bound.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 30 - Unlimited Liability in Case of Fraud
question: In Horizon Infotech LLP, partner Mr. Singhania, with the active knowledge and connivance of partner Mr. Gupta, carried on the business of the LLP with intent to defraud creditors by diverting funds to offshore personal accounts. Partner Ms. Roy had no knowledge and acted in good faith. What is the extent of liability under Section 30?
options: The liability of the LLP, Mr. Singhania, and Mr. Gupta shall be unlimited for all debts, while the liability of innocent partner Ms. Roy remains limited to her capital contribution.
All partners, including innocent partner Ms. Roy, incur unlimited personal liability jointly and severally.
The LLP cannot be held liable for criminal acts of its partners, making only Mr. Singhania personally liable.
Liability is limited to twice the capital contribution of each partner under the LLP Act.
ref: Section 30(1) and 30(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 30(1), in the event of an act carried out by an LLP or any of its partners with intent to defraud creditors, the liability of the LLP and the partners who acted with intent to defraud shall be unlimited. However, under the proviso, where any partner has acted fraudulently, the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner unless it is established that the act was done without the knowledge or authority of the LLP. An innocent partner without connivance retains limited liability.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 29 - Doctrine of Holding Out
question: Mr. Mehta, who was never a partner in Quantum Tech LLP, represented himself as a partner on social media and at a commercial trade fair. Relying on this representation, a bank granted a loan of ₹40 Lakhs to the LLP. When the LLP defaulted, the bank sued Mr. Mehta. What is Mr. Mehta's liability under Section 29?
options: Mr. Mehta is liable by holding out to the bank who has on the faith of such representation given credit to the LLP.
Mr. Mehta incurs no liability because his name was not registered in the Ministry of Corporate Affairs LLP portal.
Mr. Mehta is only liable to pay a criminal fine of ₹10,000 to the Registrar.
The bank loses its claim because it failed to inspect the public register of partners.
ref: Section 29(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 29(1) (Doctrine of Holding Out), anyone who by words spoken or written or by conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented to be a partner in an LLP, is liable to any person who has on the faith of any such representation given credit to the LLP, whether the person representing himself does or does not know that the representation has reached the creditor.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 34 - Maintenance of Books of Account & Solvency Statement
question: Every LLP is required to prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency under Section 34(2). Within what period from the closure of each financial year must this statement be prepared and filed with the Registrar in Form 8?
options: Prepared within 6 months from the end of the financial year (by Sept 30) and filed with ROC within 30 days from the end of 6 months (i.e., by October 30).
Prepared and filed within 60 days from the end of the financial year (by May 30).
Prepared within 30 days and filed along with annual return by November 30.
Mandatory only for LLPs having capital contribution exceeding ₹1 Crore.
ref: Section 34(2) and 34(3) read with Rule 24 of LLP Rules, 2009
explanation: Under Section 34(2) read with Rule 24(4), every LLP shall prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency in Form 8 within a period of 6 months from the end of each financial year (by Sept 30) and file the same with the Registrar within 30 days from the end of 6 months of the financial year (by Oct 30).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 34(4) - Mandatory Audit of LLP Accounts Threshold
question: Under Rule 24 of the Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009, an LLP is exempt from mandatory audit of its accounts if it satisfies which of the following criteria?
options: Its turnover does not exceed ₹40 Lakhs in any financial year AND its contribution does not exceed ₹25 Lakhs.
Its turnover does not exceed ₹1 Crore AND its contribution does not exceed ₹50 Lakhs.
Its turnover does not exceed ₹2 Crores regardless of contribution.
All LLPs are mandatorily required to be audited by a Chartered Accountant without exemption.
ref: Rule 24(8) of the Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009
explanation: Under Rule 24(8), an LLP whose turnover does not exceed, in any financial year, forty lakh rupees, or whose contribution does not exceed twenty-five lakh rupees, is not required to get its accounts audited. If either threshold is crossed (turnover > ₹40L or contribution > ₹25L), statutory audit by a CA in practice is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 35 - Annual Return of LLP
question: Under Section 35(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, every LLP shall file an annual return with the Registrar in Form 11 within what timeframe?
options: Within 60 days of closure of its financial year (i.e., by May 30).
Within 30 days of closure of its financial year (i.e., by April 30).
Within 180 days of closure of financial year (by September 30).
Simultaneously with the Statement of Account and Solvency on October 30.
ref: Section 35(1) of the LLP Act, 2008 read with Rule 25 of LLP Rules, 2009
explanation: Under Section 35(1) and Rule 25(1), every LLP shall file an annual return duly authenticated with the Registrar within 60 days of closure of its financial year in Form 11. For financial year ending March 31, the due date is May 30.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6 - Minimum Number of Partners & Sole Partner Liability
question: Kestrel Solutions LLP had two partners, Mr. Roy and Mr. Sen. On August 1, 2023, Mr. Sen died in an accident. Mr. Roy continued carrying on the business of the LLP as the sole partner until March 31, 2024 (8 months) without admitting a new partner. Under Section 6(2), what is Mr. Roy's legal liability for debts contracted after February 1, 2024?
options: Mr. Roy is personally liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period after the expiry of 6 months (i.e., from February 1 onwards).
The LLP stands automatically dissolved on the date of death of Mr. Sen with zero liability for Mr. Roy.
Mr. Roy's liability remains strictly limited to his capital contribution under all circumstances.
Mr. Roy must pay a fine of ₹50,000 but incurs no personal liability for business debts.
ref: Section 6(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 6(2), if at any time the number of partners of an LLP is reduced below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while the number is so reduced, the person who has the only partner of the LLP during the time that it so carries on business after those six months and has the knowledge of the fact that it is carrying on business with him alone, shall be liable personally for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 58 & Schedule III - Conversion of Private Company into LLP
question: Starling Technologies Pvt. Ltd. wishes to convert into an LLP under Section 56 read with the Third Schedule. Which of the following conditions is mandatory for such conversion?
options: All the shareholders of the company must become partners of the LLP and no one else, and there must be no subsisting security interest in its assets at the date of application.
The conversion must be approved by the Reserve Bank of India.
The company must have paid dividends consistently for the past 3 financial years.
The company must have a minimum turnover of ₹5 Crores.
ref: Section 56 read with Third Schedule (Paragraph 2 & 3) of LLP Act, 2008
explanation: Under Paragraph 2 of the Third Schedule to the LLP Act 2008, a private company may convert into an LLP only if: (a) there is no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of application; and (b) the partners of the LLP to which it converts comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 64 - Circumstances in which LLP may be Wound Up by Tribunal
question: Under Section 64 of the LLP Act, 2008, which of the following is NOT a ground on which the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) may wind up an LLP?
options: The LLP decides to distribute its profits in equal proportion rather than according to capital contribution.
The LLP is unable to pay its debts.
The number of partners of the LLP is reduced below two for a period of more than six months.
The LLP has made a default in filing with the Registrar the Statement of Account and Solvency or annual return for any five consecutive financial years.
ref: Section 64 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 64, an LLP may be wound up by Tribunal if: (a) LLP decides it be wound up; (b) number of partners reduced below 2 for >6 months; (c) LLP unable to pay debts; (d) acted against sovereignty/security of India; (e) default in filing Statement of Account & Solvency or Annual Return for 5 consecutive years; or (f) just and equitable ground. Profit sharing ratios are determined by the agreement and is not a winding up ground.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 23 - LLP Agreement & First Schedule Fallback
question: Three professionals incorporate an LLP without entering into a formal written LLP Agreement. In the absence of an agreement, how are the mutual rights and duties of the partners determined under Section 23(4)?
options: Determined by the default provisions set out in the First Schedule to the LLP Act, 2008 (including equal sharing of capital and profits, no remuneration, and equal rights in management).
Determined according to the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
The LLP is deemed illegal and dissolved by ROC immediately.
The oldest partner has absolute power to dictate all management affairs.
ref: Section 23(4) read with the First Schedule of the LLP Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 23(4), in the absence of agreement as to any matter, the mutual rights and duties of the partners and the mutual rights and duties of the LLP and the partners shall be determined by the provisions relating to that matter as set out in the First Schedule. Under First Schedule, all partners share equally in capital, profits, and management with no partner entitled to remuneration.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 24 - Cessation of Partnership Interest
question: Under Section 24(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, how may a partner resign or cease to be a partner in an LLP in the absence of an agreement?
options: By giving a notice in writing of not less than 30 days to the other partners of his intention to resign as partner.
By publishing a public notice in two national newspapers 60 days in advance.
A partner can never resign until all existing liabilities are fully repaid.
Only by obtaining an order of discharge from the NCLT.
ref: Section 24(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 24(1), a person may cease to be a partner of an LLP in accordance with an agreement with the other partners or, in the absence of agreement with the other partners as to cessation of being a partner, by giving a notice in writing of not less than thirty days to the other partners of his intention to resign as partner.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 25 - Registration of Changes in Partners
question: When a person becomes or ceases to be a partner in an LLP, or changes his name or address, within what period must the LLP file notice with the Registrar in Form 4 under Section 25(2)?
options: Within 30 days from the date he becomes or ceases to be a partner or changes his name/address.
Within 15 days from the date of the partner's resignation.
Within 60 days along with the annual return.
At the end of the financial year on March 31.
ref: Section 25(2) of the LLP Act, 2008 read with Rule 21
explanation: Under Section 25(2), an LLP shall: (a) where a person becomes or ceases to be a partner, file a notice with the Registrar within thirty days from the date he becomes or ceases to be a partner; and (b) where there is any change in the name or address of a partner, file a notice with the Registrar within thirty days of such change in Form 4.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 31 - Whistle Blowing Protection in LLP
question: An employee of Orion Biotech LLP provides vital documents to the Registrar disclosing fraudulent diversion of government research grants by the designated partners. The designated partners immediately terminate the employee's services. What protection is available to the whistleblower under Section 31 of the LLP Act, 2008?
options: No partner or employee of any LLP may be discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed or in any other manner discriminated against for providing information or assisting in an investigation.
The LLP Act provides protection only to partners, not employees.
The employee is only entitled to 3 months severance pay without reinstatement.
Whistleblower protection applies exclusively to listed companies under SEBI regulations.
ref: Section 31(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 31(2) (Whistle Blowing), no partner or employee of any LLP may be discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed or in any other manner discriminated against the terms and conditions of his LLP or employment merely because of his providing information or causing information to be provided pursuant to subsection (1).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 60 - Compromise or Arrangement by LLP
question: Under Section 60 of the LLP Act, 2008, where a compromise or arrangement is proposed between an LLP and its creditors or partners, what majority is required at the meeting convened by the Tribunal to sanction the scheme?
options: A majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or partners present and voting in person or by proxy, and sanctioned by the Tribunal.
A simple majority of total creditors by value.
Unanimous consent of all registered partners.
Approval by 90% of secured creditors only.
ref: Section 60(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 60(2), if a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of creditors, or partners, as the case may be, present and voting either in person or by proxy at the meeting, agree to any compromise or arrangement, the compromise or arrangement shall, if sanctioned by the Tribunal, be binding on all the creditors or partners and the LLP.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 11 - Incorporation Document & Registered Office
question: Under Section 11 of the LLP Act, 2008, which of the following statements regarding the Incorporation Document is INCORRECT?
options: The statement required to be filed along with the incorporation document can only be signed by an advocate; CAs and CSs are not authorized.
Two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit must subscribe their names to an incorporation document.
The incorporation document shall be filed in such manner and with such fees as may be prescribed with the Registrar.
The document must state the name of the LLP and the proposed business.
ref: Section 11(1)(c) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 11(1)(c), the statement shall be signed by an advocate, or by a Chartered Accountant or a Cost Accountant or a Company Secretary in practice, who is engaged in the formation of the LLP, and by anyone who subscribed his name to the incorporation document. Thus, CAs and CSs are fully authorized, making statement (a) incorrect.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 67 - Application of Companies Act Provisions to LLP
question: Does the Central Government have power to direct that any of the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 shall apply to any Limited Liability Partnership?
options: Yes, under Section 67(1), the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any of the provisions of the Companies Act shall apply to any LLP with such exception, modification and adaptation.
No, the LLP Act is a completely closed code and no provisions of the Companies Act can ever apply.
Yes, but only if the Supreme Court issues a writ of mandamus.
Only provisions relating to criminal trials apply automatically.
ref: Section 67(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 67(1), the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any of the provisions of the Companies Act specified in the notification shall apply to any LLP or shall apply to any LLP with such exception, modification and adaptation as may be specified in the notification.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Small LLP Classification (LLP Amendment Act 2021)
question: Under the LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021, what are the statutory thresholds for an LLP to be classified as a 'Small LLP'?
options: Contribution does not exceed ₹25 Lakhs (or prescribed up to ₹5 Cr) AND turnover for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed ₹40 Lakhs (or prescribed up to ₹50 Cr).
Contribution does not exceed ₹10 Lakhs and turnover does not exceed ₹20 Lakhs.
Contribution does not exceed ₹1 Crore with no turnover limit.
Small LLP status applies only if all partners are women.
ref: Section 2(1)(ta) of LLP Act, 2008 inserted by LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021
explanation: Under Section 2(1)(ta), 'small limited liability partnership' means an LLP: (i) the contribution of which does not exceed ₹25 Lakhs (or up to ₹5 Cr as prescribed); and (ii) the turnover of which for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed ₹40 Lakhs (or up to ₹50 Cr as prescribed). Small LLPs enjoy lower compliance and penalty burdens.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 13 - Registered Office of LLP & Change of Place
question: Sunrise Agro LLP desires to shift its registered office from the State of Maharashtra to the State of Karnataka. What is the statutory requirement under Section 13 read with Rule 17?
options: Obtain the consent of all partners, prior consent of all secured creditors, and publish a notice in two national newspapers, followed by filing Form 15 with ROC.
Only an ordinary resolution passed by majority partners without notice to creditors.
Approval of the Central Government through Ministry of Corporate Affairs after a public hearing.
Registered office cannot be shifted from one state to another under the LLP Act.
ref: Section 13(3) of LLP Act 2008 read with Rule 17 of LLP Rules, 2009
explanation: Under Rule 17, where the change of place of registered office is from one State to another, the LLP must: (a) obtain consent of all partners unless agreement provides otherwise; (b) obtain prior written consent of all secured creditors; (c) publish notice in English and vernacular newspaper; and (d) file notice with the Registrar within 30 days in Form 15.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 36 - Inspection of Documents at ROC
question: Under Section 36 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, which of the following documents filed with the Registrar are open to public inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fees?
options: Incorporation document, names of partners and changes therein, Statement of Account and Solvency, and Annual Return.
Internal minutes of meetings of partners only.
Confidential tax assessment orders and personal bank statements of partners.
No documents of an LLP are accessible to the public under any circumstances.
ref: Section 36 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
explanation: Under Section 36, the incorporation document, names of partners and changes therein, Statement of Account and Solvency, and annual return filed by an LLP with the Registrar shall be available for inspection by any person in the business hours of the Registrar on payment of prescribed fees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Minimum Threshold for Initiating CIRP
question: Under Section 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC), what is the minimum default amount required to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor as per the Central Government notification currently in force?
options: ₹1 Crore (One Crore Rupees).
₹1 Lakh (One Lakh Rupees).
₹10 Lakhs (Ten Lakh Rupees).
₹50 Lakhs (Fifty Lakh Rupees).
ref: Section 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Notification S.O. 1205(E) dated 24.03.2020)
