explanation: Under Section 4 of the IBC, 2016, the default threshold for initiating CIRP was originally ₹1 Lakh. By notification dated March 24, 2020, the Central Government raised the minimum amount of default to ₹1 Crore in order to prevent MSMEs and other corporate entities from being pushed into insolvency for small defaults.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 7 - Initiation of CIRP by Financial Creditors
question: A consortium of financial creditors comprising State Bank of India (holding 45% debt), Bank of Baroda (holding 30% debt), and Punjab National Bank (holding 25% debt) issues a recall notice to Krrish Infra Ltd. SBI desires to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of IBC, 2016. Can SBI file the application alone without joining the other consortium members?
options: Yes, a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors may file an application for initiating CIRP against a corporate debtor before the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) when a default has occurred.
No, unanimous consent of all consortium members is mandatory under Section 7.
No, only lead bank holding at least 51% debt can file an application.
An application can only be filed after issuing a 90-day winding up notice.
ref: Section 7(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 7(1) of the IBC, a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors, or any other person on behalf of the financial creditor, may file an application for initiating CIRP against a corporate debtor before the Adjudicating Authority when a default has occurred. Consortium consent is not a statutory prerequisite under Section 7.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 8 & 9 - Initiation of CIRP by Operational Creditor & Pre-existing Dispute
question: Falcon Logistics delivers goods worth ₹1.2 Crores to Radiant Appliances Ltd. Due to quality defects, Radiant Appliances sent an email on March 5 disputing the invoice and debiting ₹40 Lakhs. Falcon Logistics issued a demand notice under Section 8 of IBC on April 10. Radiant replied on April 18 pointing out the pre-existing dispute regarding quality defects. Falcon Logistics files a Section 9 application before NCLT. How shall the NCLT decide?
options: The NCLT shall reject the application under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) because there is a genuine pre-existing dispute raised prior to the issuance of the demand notice.
The NCLT must admit the application because the invoice amount exceeds the ₹1 Crore threshold.
The NCLT must appoint an Interim Resolution Professional and ask the IRP to adjudicate the quality dispute.
The NCLT will direct Radiant Appliances to deposit 50% in court before examining the dispute.
ref: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC read with Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd. (SC)
explanation: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Mobilox Innovations, if notice of a pre-existing dispute has been received by the operational creditor or there is a record of dispute in the information utility prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the Adjudicating Authority must reject the application. IBC is not a debt collection forum.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 14 - Moratorium Effect & Exemptions
question: Upon admission of a CIRP application against Orbit Power Ltd., the NCLT declares a moratorium under Section 14. Which of the following actions is strictly prohibited during the moratorium period?
options: Institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel.
Supply of essential goods or services (such as electricity, water, telecommunications) to the corporate debtor.
Transactions by the corporate debtor in furtherance of its operations under the direction of the Resolution Professional.
Invocation of a performance bank guarantee given by a financial institution.
ref: Section 14(1) and 14(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 14(1)(a), the declaration of moratorium strictly prohibits the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor. Conversely, essential goods/services cannot be terminated (Sec 14(2)) and performance bank guarantees are exempt from moratorium under the amended Section 14(3).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 21 & 24 - Committee of Creditors (CoC) Composition & Voting Share
question: In the CIRP of Titan Steel Ltd., the Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises Financial Creditor A (voting share 50%), Financial Creditor B (voting share 20%), and Financial Creditor C (a related party of the corporate debtor having 30% financial debt). What is the voting right of Financial Creditor C in the CoC meetings under Section 21(2)?
options: Financial Creditor C has zero right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the Committee of Creditors, and the remaining creditors' voting shares will be normalized to 100%.
Financial Creditor C can participate and vote on ordinary matters but not on resolution plan approval.
Financial Creditor C has equal voting rights provided NCLT grants permission.
Financial Creditor C votes with 50% discount on its voting power.
ref: First proviso to Section 21(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under the first proviso to Section 21(2), a financial creditor or the authorised representative of the financial creditor, if it is a related party of the corporate debtor, shall not have any right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the Committee of Creditors. Its debt is excluded when computing total voting share.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 30(4) - CoC Voting Threshold for Resolution Plan
question: A resolution plan submitted by Star Mining Ltd. in respect of a corporate debtor is put to vote in the CoC meeting. Creditors holding 64% voting share vote in favor of the plan, 20% vote against, and 16% abstain. What is the fate of the resolution plan under Section 30(4)?
options: The resolution plan is rejected because approval of a resolution plan mandatorily requires not less than 66% of voting share of the financial creditors.
The resolution plan is approved because 64% out of participating creditors (64 / 84 = 76.19%) exceeds the 66% threshold.
The plan is approved because simple majority (51%) is sufficient under the amended rules.
The Resolution Professional can exercise a casting vote to approve the plan.
ref: Section 30(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 30(4), the Committee of Creditors may approve a resolution plan by a vote of not less than sixty-six percent (66%) of voting share of the financial creditors. The percentage is calculated based on the total voting share of the CoC, not merely those present and voting. Since 64% < 66%, the resolution plan stands rejected.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 29A - Persons Ineligible to be Resolution Applicants
question: Mr. Singhal submitted a resolution plan for an insolvent textile company. An investigation reveals that Mr. Singhal was a promoter of an entity whose account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) by a commercial bank 18 months prior to the CIRP commencement date, and such default continues. Is Mr. Singhal eligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 29A(c)?
options: No, he is disqualified under Section 29A(c) as his account has been classified as NPA for a period of at least one year prior to the commencement of CIRP, unless he pays all overdue amounts with interest before submitting the plan.
Yes, he is fully eligible provided he pays a processing deposit of ₹50 Lakhs to the CoC.
Yes, the NPA disqualification applies only to willful defaulters, not ordinary NPA promoters.
Disqualification under Section 29A applies only to foreign citizens.
ref: Section 29A(c) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 29A(c), a person is ineligible to submit a resolution plan if at the time of submission of the plan has an account, or an account of a corporate debtor under his management or control, classified as NPA for a period of at least one year prior to the date of commencement of CIRP, and such person has failed to pay in full all overdue amounts with interest thereon and other charges before submission of the plan.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53 - Distribution of Assets (Waterfall Mechanism)
question: In the liquidation of Galaxy Electronics Ltd., the liquidator realizes ₹100 Crores. The claims include: (a) CIRP costs and liquidation costs: ₹5 Crores; (b) Workmen dues (past 24 months) and secured debts of creditors who relinquished security: ₹40 Crores; (c) Wages of employees other than workmen (past 12 months): ₹10 Crores; (d) Central Government taxes: ₹15 Crores. Under Section 53, who gets paid first after meeting the insolvency resolution process costs?
options: Workmen's dues for 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor in the event such secured creditor has relinquished security to the liquidation estate, ranking equally.
Central Government taxes under the sovereign priority rule.
Unsecured financial creditors.
Wages and salaries of non-workmen employees for 12 months.
ref: Section 53(1)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 53(1) (Waterfall Mechanism): (a) CIRP costs and liquidation costs are paid first in full; (b) Next, workmen's dues for the period of 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date AND debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security under Section 52 rank equally (pari passu); (c) Wages and unpaid dues to employees other than workmen for 12 months; (d) Unsecured financial debts; (e) Government dues and remaining secured debts.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 12 - Time-limit for Completion of CIRP
question: Under Section 12 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, what is the statutory period for completing the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), including any extension and litigation period?
options: Mandatorily completed within 180 days, extendable once by the Adjudicating Authority by up to 90 days upon CoC approval (66%), with overall completion mandatorily within 330 days from insolvency commencement date including legal proceedings.
Completed within 90 days, extendable by another 90 days without any outer cap.
Completed within 365 days with no discretion for NCLT to extend.
Completed within 60 days for all public companies.
ref: Section 12(1), 12(2) and 12(3) second proviso of the IBC, 2016
explanation: Under Section 12(1), the CIRP shall be completed within a period of 180 days. Under Section 12(3), NCLT may extend this period by a maximum of 90 days if instructed by CoC with 66% majority. Under the second proviso to Section 12(3), the CIRP shall mandatorily be completed within a period of 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, including any extension and time taken in legal proceedings.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 43 - Preferential Transactions and Relevant Time
question: During CIRP, the Resolution Professional finds that the corporate debtor transferred an unencumbered commercial property to an unsecured financial creditor (who is a non-related party) to extinguish a 3-year-old loan, 8 months prior to the insolvency commencement date. Under Section 43, what is the relevant 'look-back period' for avoiding preferential transactions for non-related parties?
options: A period of one year preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of six months preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of two years preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of three years preceding the admission order.
ref: Section 43(4)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 43(4), a preference shall be deemed to be given at a relevant time if: (a) it is given to a related party during the period of two years preceding the insolvency commencement date; OR (b) it is given to a person other than a related party during the period of one year preceding the insolvency commencement date. Since 8 months < 1 year, the transaction is avoidable as a preference.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 45 - Undervalued Transactions
question: The corporate debtor gifted machinery valued at ₹2 Crores to a relative of the promoter for a consideration of ₹10 Lakhs, 18 months prior to the insolvency commencement date. Can the Resolution Professional apply to the Adjudicating Authority to declare this transaction void under Section 45?
options: Yes, because for transactions with a related party, the look-back period for undervalued transactions under Section 46(1) is two years preceding the insolvency commencement date.
No, the look-back period for undervalued transactions is strictly capped at one year for all parties.
No, because consideration was paid, and any positive consideration precludes undervaluation.
Only the Central Government can file an avoidance application under Section 45.
ref: Section 45(1) and Section 46(1)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 45, where a transaction is undervalued, the RP may make an application to NCLT. Under Section 46(1), the relevant period is: (a) one year preceding insolvency commencement date for non-related persons; and (b) two years preceding insolvency commencement date where the transaction was with a related party. Since 18 months < 2 years, it is an avoidable undervalued transaction.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 66 - Fraudulent Trading or Wrongful Trading
question: During CIRP, forensic audit reveals that the directors of the corporate debtor continued to accept customer advance payments knowing fully well that the company had no manufacturing capability and insolvency was inevitable. What liability can the NCLT impose under Section 66(2)?
options: The NCLT may direct that such director shall be personally liable to make such contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor as it thinks fit, because before the insolvency commencement date he knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding CIRP.
The NCLT can only disqualify the directors from future directorships under Section 164 of Companies Act.
The directors incur criminal liability only with no financial contribution to corporate assets.
The liability is limited to the unpaid share capital on their equity shares.
ref: Section 66(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 66(2) (Wrongful Trading), on an application made by the RP, the Adjudicating Authority may direct that a director or partner shall be liable to make such contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor as it may deem fit, if before the insolvency commencement date, such person knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding commencement of CIRP and failed to exercise due diligence.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 54A - Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)
question: Under Chapter III-A of IBC (inserted in 2021), Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) is available exclusively to which category of corporate debtors, and what is the minimum default threshold?
options: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) under the MSMED Act, 2006, with a minimum default threshold of ₹10 Lakhs.
All listed public companies with default above ₹10 Crores.
Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with assets above ₹500 Crores.
Any corporate debtor having turnover below ₹100 Crores with default of ₹1 Crore.
ref: Section 54A(1) and 54A(2) of IBC, 2016 read with MCA Notification S.O. 1543(E)
explanation: Under Section 54A, PPIRP is available exclusively to corporate debtors classified as Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises under Section 7(1) of the MSMED Act, 2006. The Central Government has notified a minimum default threshold of ₹10 Lakhs for initiating PPIRP.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 12A - Withdrawal of Application Admitted under CIRP
question: After an application for CIRP against Pioneer Polymers Ltd. has been admitted by the NCLT, the corporate debtor and the applicant creditor reach an out-of-court settlement. Under Section 12A, what condition must be satisfied to withdraw the admitted CIRP application?
options: The Adjudicating Authority may allow the withdrawal of application on an application made by the applicant with the approval of ninety percent (90%) voting share of the Committee of Creditors.
Approval by 66% voting share of the Committee of Creditors is sufficient.
Unanimous approval of all creditors and all equity shareholders.
Withdrawal is strictly prohibited once the CIRP is admitted under any circumstances.
ref: Section 12A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 12A, the Adjudicating Authority may allow the withdrawal of application admitted under section 7 or section 9 or section 10, on an application made by the applicant with the approval of ninety percent (90%) voting share of the Committee of Creditors, in such manner as may be prescribed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 33 - Initiation of Liquidation by NCLT
question: Under Section 33(1) of IBC, which of the following events triggers an order for liquidation of the corporate debtor by the Adjudicating Authority?
options: Where the Adjudicating Authority does not receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the CIRP period, or rejects the resolution plan under Section 31 for non-compliance.
Where any single creditor with 5% debt demands liquidation in the first meeting of CoC.
Where the corporate debtor's factory experiences a 30-day labor strike.
Where the net worth of the company becomes negative during the CIRP.
ref: Section 33(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 33(1), where the Adjudicating Authority: (a) before the expiry of the insolvency resolution process period does not receive a resolution plan under Section 30(6); or (b) rejects the resolution plan under Section 31 for the non-compliance of the requirements, it shall pass an order requiring the corporate debtor to be liquidated.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 17 - Management of Affairs by Interim Resolution Professional
question: From the date of appointment of the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) under Section 17, what is the status of the Board of Directors of the corporate debtor?
options: The powers of the Board of Directors or partners of the corporate debtor stand suspended and are exercised by the IRP, and officers/managers shall report to the IRP.
The Board of Directors continues to exercise day-to-day management subject to quarterly reporting to IRP.
The Board of Directors is permanently dissolved and their directorship DINs are cancelled.
The Managing Director becomes an employee of the NCLT.
ref: Section 17(1)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 17(1)(b), from the date of appointment of the IRP, the powers of the Board of Directors or the partners of the corporate debtor, as the case may be, shall stand suspended and be exercised by the interim resolution professional. The management of affairs vests entirely in the IRP.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 18 & 25 - Information Memorandum & Duty of RP
question: Under Section 29 of the IBC, 2016 read with Regulation 36 of IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, within what timeframe must the Resolution Professional prepare and submit the Information Memorandum (IM) to each member of the CoC?
options: In electronic form to each member of the committee within 90 days from the insolvency commencement date.
Within 14 days from the date of appointment of the IRP.
Within 180 days along with the resolution plan.
Only after the resolution applicant pays the earnest money deposit.
ref: Regulation 36(1) of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016
explanation: Under Regulation 36(1) of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, the Resolution Professional shall submit the information memorandum in electronic form to each member of the Committee within 90 days from the insolvency commencement date, subject to obtaining an undertaking of confidentiality.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 32A - Liability for Prior Offences upon Resolution Plan Approval
question: Under Section 32A of IBC, what is the effect of approval of a resolution plan on the criminal liability of the corporate debtor for offences committed prior to the commencement of CIRP?
options: The liability of the corporate debtor for an offence committed prior to the commencement of CIRP shall cease, and the corporate debtor shall not be prosecuted from the date the resolution plan is approved by NCLT, provided the new management is not a related party of the erstwhile promoters.
The corporate debtor remains permanently liable to pay all criminal fines levied prior to CIRP.
The new resolution applicant assumes criminal personal liability for past environmental and tax offences.
Section 32A grants complete immunity to the erstwhile promoter directors from personal criminal trial.
ref: Section 32A(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Manish Kumar v. Union of India)
explanation: Under Section 32A(1), the liability of a corporate debtor for an offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP shall cease, and it shall not be prosecuted, if a resolution plan approved by NCLT results in change of management to a person who was not a promoter or in control or related party. However, individual past officers remain liable for their personal criminal acts.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 5(8) - Definition of Financial Debt (Allottees as Financial Creditors)
question: Under the Explanation to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, 2016, how are home-buyers / allottees under a real estate project classified, and what is the minimum threshold to file an application under Section 7?
options: Any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project is deemed to be a financial debt, and an application under Section 7 must be filed jointly by not less than 100 of such allottees or not less than 10% of the total number of such allottees under the same real estate project, whichever is less.
Home-buyers are operational creditors and must issue a Section 8 demand notice individually.
A single allottee with unpaid amount of ₹50 Lakhs can file a Section 7 application independently.
Home-buyers are equity partners and have no locus standi to initiate CIRP.
ref: Explanation to Section 5(8)(f) and second proviso to Section 7(1) of IBC, 2016
explanation: Under Explanation to Section 5(8)(f), any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project is deemed to be financial debt. Under the second proviso to Section 7(1), for allottees under a real estate project, an application shall be filed jointly by not less than one hundred of such allottees under the same project or not less than ten per cent of the total number of such allottees, whichever is less.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 65 - Fraudulent or Malicious Initiation of Proceedings
question: If any person initiates the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process fraudulently or with malicious intent for any purpose other than for the resolution of insolvency, what penalty is prescribed under Section 65(1)?
options: The Adjudicating Authority may impose upon such person a penalty which shall not be less than ₹1 Lakh, but may extend to ₹1 Crore.
Mandatory imprisonment for a period of not less than 5 years without option of fine.
Debarment from filing any cases before High Courts for 10 years.
Civil damages equal to 10% of the corporate debtor's total debt.
ref: Section 65(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
explanation: Under Section 65(1), if any person initiates the insolvency resolution process or liquidation proceedings fraudulently or with malicious intent for any purpose other than for the resolution of insolvency, or liquidation, the Adjudicating Authority may impose upon such person a penalty which shall not be less than one lakh rupees, but may extend to one crore rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 11B - Power of SEBI to Issue Directions & Impound Proceeds
question: Under Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Act, 1992, which of the following measures can SEBI direct against an intermediary or market participant in the interests of investors or orderly market development?
options: Suspend the trading of any security in a recognized stock exchange, restrain persons from accessing the securities market, and direct impounding and retention of all proceeds or securities involved in the violation.
Direct the compulsory dissolution of the corporate entity without reference to NCLT.
Cancel the Indian passport of the company's directors.
Order military custody of the company's premises.
ref: Section 11(4) and Section 11B of the SEBI Act, 1992
explanation: Under Section 11(4) and 11B, SEBI has comprehensive powers to issue directions including: (a) suspending trading of any security; (b) restraining persons from accessing the securities market; (c) impounding and retaining proceeds; and (d) directing attachment of bank accounts for up to 90 days.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15G - Penalty for Insider Trading
question: An insider of a listed entity trades in the securities of the company on the basis of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) and earns unlawful profits of ₹8 Crores. Under Section 15G of the SEBI Act, 1992, what is the maximum monetary penalty that can be imposed by the Adjudicating Officer?
options: A penalty which shall not be less than ₹10 Lakhs, but which may extend to ₹25 Crores or three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading, whichever is higher (i.e. up to ₹25 Crores or ₹24 Crores -> max ₹25 Crores).
Fixed penalty of ₹1 Crore only.
A penalty strictly capped at double the investment value.
Fine up to ₹50 Lakhs with mandatory 7 years imprisonment.
ref: Section 15G of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
explanation: Under Section 15G, if any insider deals in securities on the basis of UPSI or communicates UPSI, he shall be liable to a penalty which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees, but which may extend to twenty-five crore rupees or three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading, whichever is higher.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15T & 15Z - Appeal to SAT and Supreme Court
question: An order imposing a monetary penalty is passed by the Adjudicating Officer of SEBI on May 2. By what date must the aggrieved entity file an appeal before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) under Section 15T, and within what period may an appeal against SAT order be filed to the Supreme Court under Section 15Z?
options: Appeal to SAT within 45 days from the date of receipt of copy of order; Appeal against SAT order to Supreme Court on question of law within 60 days from communication of order.
Appeal to SAT within 30 days; Appeal to Supreme Court within 30 days.
Appeal to SAT within 60 days; Appeal to Supreme Court within 90 days.
Appeal to SAT within 15 days; Appeal to High Court within 30 days.
ref: Section 15T(3) and Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, 1992
explanation: Under Section 15T(3), every appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal shall be filed within a period of 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order is received. Under Section 15Z, any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Securities Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court for any question of law arising out of such order within 60 days from the date of communication.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 17 - Board Composition & Independent Directors
question: Under Regulation 17(1) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, if the Chairperson of the Board of Directors of a listed entity is a non-executive director and is a promoter or related to any promoter, what proportion of the Board must comprise Independent Directors?
options: At least half (50%) of the Board of Directors shall consist of Independent Directors.
At least one-third (33.33%) of the Board of Directors.
At least two-thirds (66.67%) of the Board of Directors.
Only 2 independent directors are required regardless of promoter relation.
ref: Regulation 17(1)(b) proviso of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 17(1)(b), where the chairperson of the board of directors is a non-executive director, at least one-third of the board of directors shall comprise of independent directors. However, under the proviso, where the non-executive chairperson is a promoter of the listed entity or is related to any promoter or person occupying management positions, at least half (50%) of the board of directors shall consist of independent directors.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 18 - Audit Committee Composition & Quorum
question: Under Regulation 18 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, which of the following requirements regarding the Audit Committee of a listed entity is MANDATORY?
options: The Audit Committee shall have minimum 3 directors as members, at least two-thirds of the members shall be independent directors, and the Chairperson shall be an independent director who shall be present at AGM.
All members of the Audit Committee must be executive directors with accounting degrees.
Audit Committee quorum is one director personally present.
Audit Committee is required to meet only once every financial year.
ref: Regulation 18(1) and 18(2) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 18(1), the Audit Committee must have minimum 3 directors, at least two-thirds of the members shall be independent directors (for listed entities with SR equity shares, all members must be independent), and the Chairperson shall be an independent director present at the AGM. Quorum is two members or one-third, whichever is greater, with at least two independent directors.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 23 - Material Related Party Transactions (RPT)
question: Under Regulation 23 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, a transaction with a related party shall be considered 'material' if the transaction(s) to be entered into individually or taken together with previous transactions during a financial year exceeds which threshold?
options: ₹1,000 Crore OR 10% of the annual consolidated turnover of the listed entity as per the last audited financial statements, whichever is lower.
₹100 Crore or 5% of turnover, whichever is higher.
10% of net worth of the holding company exclusively.
₹500 Crore regardless of consolidated turnover.
ref: Regulation 23(1) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 (as amended)
explanation: Under amended Regulation 23(1), a transaction with a related party shall be considered material if the transaction(s) to be entered into individually or taken together with previous transactions during a financial year, exceeds ₹1,000 Crore or 10% of the annual consolidated turnover of the listed entity as per the last audited financial statements, whichever is lower. Prior shareholder approval by ordinary resolution is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 30 - Disclosure of Material Events to Stock Exchanges
question: A listed pharmaceutical company discovers an unexpected fire accident causing severe damage of ₹60 Crores to its active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing unit. Under Regulation 30 read with Schedule III of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, within what timeframe must the listed entity disclose this material event to stock exchanges?
options: As soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from the occurrence of the event (or 12 hours if originating from within the company).
Within 7 days of completion of the insurance surveyor's assessment.
At the immediate next quarterly financial results announcement.
Within 48 hours of Board approval of the restoration plan.
ref: Regulation 30(6) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 (as amended in 2023)
explanation: Under Regulation 30(6) as amended, the listed entity shall disclose to the stock exchange(s) all material events as soon as reasonably possible and in any case not later than: (i) 30 minutes from closure of Board meeting for decisions; (ii) 12 hours from occurrence if originating from within; (iii) 24 hours from occurrence if not originating from within.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (PIT) Reg 2(1)(n) - Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)
question: Under Regulation 2(1)(n) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, which of the following is explicitly deemed to be Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)?
options: Financial results, dividends, change in capital structure, mergers, de-mergers, acquisitions, delistings, disposals and expansion of business, and changes in Key Managerial Personnel.
Routine quarterly sales volume disclosures published on company website.
Public press releases announcing award of industry excellence trophies.
Employee retirement notices below managerial cadre.
ref: Regulation 2(1)(n) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 2(1)(n), 'unpublished price sensitive information' means any information, relating to a company or its securities, directly or indirectly, that is not generally available which upon becoming generally available is likely to materially affect the price of securities, including: financial results, dividends, change in capital structure, M&A/restructuring, and changes in KMP.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (PIT) Reg 9 - Trading Window Closure Period
question: Under Clause 4 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9 of SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015, trading window restrictions shall mandatorily be applied by listed entities from which date until when?
options: From the end of every quarter till 48 hours after the declaration of financial results.
From 7 days before the Board meeting till 24 hours after results declaration.
Only on the exact day of the Board meeting approving financial statements.
From the beginning of the financial year till the Annual General Meeting.
ref: Clause 4 of Schedule B of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Clause 4 of Schedule B (Minimum Standards for Code of Conduct), trading restriction period shall be made applicable from the end of every quarter till 48 hours after the declaration of financial results. Designated persons and their immediate relatives are prohibited from trading during this window closure.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (SAST) Reg 3 - Substantial Acquisition Threshold (Trigger Limit)
question: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (SAST), what is the threshold of voting rights that triggers the mandatory obligation to make a public announcement of an open offer to acquire shares from public shareholders?
options: Acquiring shares or voting rights which taken together with existing holdings entitle the acquirer and PACs to exercise 25% or more of voting rights in the target company.
Acquiring 15% or more of voting rights.
Acquiring 51% or more of paid-up equity share capital.
Acquiring any voting rights exceeding 5% in a single financial year.
ref: Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011
explanation: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, no acquirer shall acquire shares or voting rights in a target company which taken together with shares or voting rights held by him and by persons acting in concert (PAC) with him in such target company, entitle them to exercise twenty-five per cent (25%) or more of the voting rights, unless the acquirer makes a public announcement of an open offer.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (SAST) Reg 3(2) - Creeping Acquisition Limit
question: An acquirer holds 38% voting rights in an equity listed company. During FY 2024-25, the acquirer desires to purchase additional shares from the open market without triggering a mandatory open offer. What is the maximum percentage of voting rights the acquirer can acquire under the 'creeping acquisition' provision of Regulation 3(2)?
options: Up to 5% of voting rights in that financial year, provided the acquisition does not result in total holding exceeding maximum permissible non-public shareholding (75%).
Up to 10% of voting rights in any financial year.
Up to 2% of voting rights every quarter.
Zero additional shares can be acquired without an open offer once holding exceeds 25%.
ref: Regulation 3(2) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011
explanation: Under Regulation 3(2), an acquirer who holds 25% or more but less than maximum permissible non-public shareholding (75%) may acquire additional shares or voting rights entitling him to exercise more than 5% of voting rights in any financial year only by making an open offer. Therefore, acquisitions up to 5% in a financial year (creeping acquisition) are permitted without an open offer.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (SAST) Reg 7 - Offer Size in Open Offer
question: Under Regulation 7(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011, what is the mandatory minimum offer size that an acquirer must make in a public announcement of an open offer under Regulation 3 or Regulation 4?
options: At least twenty-six percent (26%) of total shares of the target company as of tenth working day from the closure of the tendering period.
Exactly twenty percent (20%) of the paid-up share capital.
Fifty-one percent (51%) of total voting shares.
Ten percent (10%) of the public shareholding.
ref: Regulation 7(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011
explanation: Under Regulation 7(1), the open offer for acquiring shares to be made by the acquirer and PAC under regulation 3 and regulation 4 shall be for at least twenty-six per cent (26%) of total shares of the target company, as of tenth working day from closure of the tendering period.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (ICDR) Reg 6 - Eligibility Requirements for IPO
question: An unlisted company planning an Initial Public Offering (IPO) of equity shares must satisfy which financial criteria under Regulation 6(1) of SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018?
options: Net tangible assets of at least ₹3 Cr in each of preceding 3 full years; Average operating profit of at least ₹15 Cr during preceding 3 years; Net worth of at least ₹1 Cr in each of preceding 3 full years.
Net tangible assets of at least ₹10 Cr and turnover of ₹100 Cr in the immediately preceding year.
Net profit of at least ₹50 Cr in the current year regardless of past history.
Continuous dividend payment for 10 consecutive years.
ref: Regulation 6(1) of SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018
explanation: Under Regulation 6(1) (Profitability Route), the issuer must have: (a) Net tangible assets of at least ₹3 Crores in each of the preceding 3 full years (max 50% monetary assets); (b) Average operating profit of at least ₹15 Crores during the 3 most profitable years out of preceding 5 years; (c) Net worth of at least ₹1 Crore in each of the preceding 3 full years.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (ICDR) Reg 6(2) - QIB Book-Building Alternative Route
question: An issuer company not satisfying the profitability track record under Regulation 6(1) can still undertake an IPO of equity shares under Regulation 6(2) of SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018 provided it complies with which condition?
options: The issue is made through the book-building process and the issuer undertakes to allot at least 75% of the net offer to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs), and refund full subscription if minimum QIB allotment is not met.
The issue is made exclusively to retail individual investors with 50% discount.
The issuer obtains an unconditional guarantee from the Reserve Bank of India.
All directors deposit 100% of their personal assets in an escrow account with SEBI.
ref: Regulation 6(2) of SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018
explanation: Under Regulation 6(2), an issuer not satisfying the conditions of Regulation 6(1) shall be eligible to make an initial public offer only if the issue is made through the book-building process and the issuer undertakes to allot, at least seventy-five per cent (75%) of the net offer to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) and to refund the full subscription money if it fails to make the said minimum allotment.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (ICDR) Reg 14 & 16 - Minimum Promoters Contribution & Lock-in
question: In an Initial Public Offering (IPO) of equity shares, what is the mandatory minimum promoters' contribution required, and what is the lock-in period under Regulation 14 and 16 of SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018?
options: Promoters shall contribute not less than 20% of post-issue capital, locked in for 18 months (or 3 years if project involves capital expenditure), and excess promoters' holding locked in for 6 months.
Promoters must hold 51% post-issue capital locked in for 5 years.
Promoters must contribute 10% locked in for 1 year.
No lock-in applies if shares are held in dematerialized format.
ref: Regulation 14 and Regulation 16 of SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018 (as amended)
explanation: Under Regulation 14, minimum promoters' contribution shall not be less than 20% of post-issue capital. Under amended Regulation 16, minimum promoters' contribution is locked in for 18 months from date of allotment (reduced from 3 years for eligible issuers), and any excess promoter shareholding is locked in for 6 months (reduced from 1 year).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (PIT) Reg 3 - Communication of UPSI & Legitimate Purpose
question: Under Regulation 3(2A) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, communicating unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI) in furtherance of 'legitimate purposes' is legally permitted. How must the Board of Directors define 'legitimate purpose'?
options: The Board shall formulate a policy for determination of 'legitimate purposes' as part of Codes of Fair Disclosure, which shall include sharing of UPSI in ordinary course of business by an insider with partners, collaborators, lenders, customers, suppliers, merchant bankers, legal advisors, auditors, or insolvency professionals.
Legitimate purpose is defined exclusively by SEBI on a case-to-case basis via formal no-objection letters.
Sharing UPSI is never permitted under any circumstance, even with statutory auditors.
Sharing UPSI is legitimate only when done via televised news interviews.
ref: Regulation 3(2A) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 3(2A), the board of directors of a listed company shall formulate a policy for determination of 'legitimate purposes' as a part of the codes of fair disclosure. It shall include sharing of UPSI in the ordinary course of business with collaborators, lenders, customers, suppliers, merchant bankers, legal advisors, auditors, or insolvency professionals, provided sharing is not done to evade PIT prohibitions.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 27 - Quarterly Corporate Governance Compliance Report
question: Under Regulation 27(2) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, within how many days from the end of each quarter must a listed entity submit a quarterly corporate governance compliance report to the recognized stock exchange(s)?
options: Within 21 days from the end of each quarter.
Within 15 days from the end of each quarter.
Within 45 days along with financial results.
Within 30 days from the closure of the quarter.
ref: Regulation 27(2)(a) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 27(2)(a), the listed entity shall submit a quarterly compliance report on corporate governance in the format as specified by the Board from time to time to the recognized stock exchange(s) within twenty-one (21) days from the end of each quarter.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15A - Penalty for Failure to Furnish Information/Returns
question: If any person who is required under the SEBI Act or rules to furnish any document, return or report to SEBI fails to furnish the same, what penalty is leviable under Section 15A(a)?
options: A penalty which shall not be less than ₹1 Lakh, but which may extend to ₹1 Lakh for each day during which such failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹1 Crore.
Fixed penalty of ₹50,000 per violation.
Suspension of trading in shares for 3 years.
Immediate imprisonment for 6 months.
ref: Section 15A(a) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
explanation: Under Section 15A(a), if any person fails to furnish any document, return or report to the Board, he shall be liable to a penalty which shall not be less than one lakh rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees for each day during which such failure continues subject to a maximum of one crore rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 19 - Nomination & Remuneration Committee
question: Under Regulation 19 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, what is the mandatory composition of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee for a listed entity?
options: The committee shall comprise of at least 3 directors, all directors of the committee shall be non-executive directors, and at least two-thirds of the directors shall be independent directors.
The committee must consist of 5 directors including the Chief Executive Officer.
Only executive directors can form the Nomination and Remuneration Committee.
At least half the committee must be independent directors.
ref: Regulation 19(1) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 (as amended)
explanation: Under Regulation 19(1) of SEBI (LODR), the Nomination and Remuneration Committee shall: (a) comprise of at least three directors; (b) all directors of the committee shall be non-executive directors; (c) at least two-thirds of the directors shall be independent directors; and (d) Chairperson of the committee shall be an independent director.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 24 - Offences & Penal Provisions by Courts
question: Under Section 24(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992, if any person contravenes or attempts to contravene or abets the contravention of the provisions of this Act or of any rules or regulations made thereunder, what criminal punishment can be imposed by a Court of competent jurisdiction?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, which may extend to twenty-five crore rupees, or with both.
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to ₹1 Crore.
Imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to ₹50 Lakhs.
Strictly monetary fine with zero provision for imprisonment.
ref: Section 24(1) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
explanation: Under Section 24(1), without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under this Act, if any person contravenes or attempts to contravene or abets the contravention of the provisions of this Act or of any rules or regulations made thereunder, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, which may extend to twenty-five crore rupees or with both.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 2(v) - Residential Status under FEMA
question: Mr. Rohan, an Indian citizen, resided in India for 210 days during FY 2022-23. On May 10, 2023, he went to London to take up an employment contract for a duration of 3 years. What is Mr. Rohan's residential status under Section 2(v) of FEMA, 1999 for FY 2023-24?
options: Person Resident Outside India (PROI) with effect from May 10, 2023, because he went outside India for taking up employment outside India.
Person Resident in India (PRII) for the entire FY 2023-24 because his stay in India in FY 2022-23 exceeded 182 days.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident as defined under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Dual resident entitled to relief under double tax avoidance agreements.
ref: Section 2(v)(i)(A) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 2(v)(i), 'person resident in India' means a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year, but DOES NOT INCLUDE a person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India for or on taking up employment outside India (Clause A). Since Rohan went abroad for employment, he becomes a Person Resident Outside India (PROI) from the date of departure.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 5 & FEM (CAT) Rules - Prohibited Current Account Transactions
question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, which of the following current account transactions is completely PROHIBITED under Schedule I?
options: Remittance out of lottery winnings, racing/riding income, purchase of lottery tickets, football pools, and sweepstakes.
Remittance for cultural tours.
Remittance for hiring transponders for TV channels.
Remittance of commission on exports under Rupee State Credit Route.
ref: Schedule I of FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 read with Section 5
explanation: Under Schedule I of FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, remittance out of lottery winnings, remittance of income from racing/riding or any other hobby, remittance for purchase of lottery tickets, banned/proscribed magazines, football pools, sweepstakes, etc., are completely prohibited.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Schedule III & LRS - Liberalised Remittance Scheme Ceiling
question: Mr. Kapoor, an individual resident in India, intends to remit foreign exchange abroad for his son's overseas education and his family holiday. Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) of RBI read with Schedule III of FEM (CAT) Rules, what is the annual permissible ceiling for all permissible current and capital account transactions per financial year?
options: Up to USD 2,50,000 (Two Hundred Fifty Thousand US Dollars) or its equivalent per financial year (April-March) without prior RBI approval.
Up to USD 1,00,000 per financial year.
Up to USD 5,00,000 per calendar year.
Unlimited remittances provided TCS at 20% is collected.
ref: Schedule III of FEM (CAT) Rules, 2000 read with RBI A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars on LRS
explanation: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), resident individuals are freely permitted to remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permissible current or capital account transactions or a combination of both without prior approval of RBI. Any remittance exceeding USD 2,50,000 requires prior approval of the Reserve Bank.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6 - Permissible Capital Account Transactions
question: Which of the following is explicitly classified as a 'Capital Account Transaction' under Section 2(e) read with Section 6 of FEMA, 1999?
options: Investment in foreign securities by a resident Indian, raising of foreign currency loans (ECBs), and transfer of immovable property outside India by a person resident in India.
Payment due as interest on loans and as net income from investments.
Remittance for living expenses of parents residing abroad.
Payment due in connection with foreign trade and short-term banking credit facilities.
ref: Section 2(e) and Section 6(3) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 2(e), 'capital account transaction' means a transaction which alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India or assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India. Foreign security investments, foreign loans (ECBs), and overseas immovable property transfers alter such balance sheets and are capital account transactions.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] FDI Policy - Prohibited Sectors for Foreign Direct Investment
question: Under the Consolidated Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Policy and Non-Debt Instruments (NDI) Rules, 2019, in which of the following sectors is Foreign Direct Investment completely PROHIBITED?
options: Lottery business, gambling and betting, chit funds, Nidhi company, trading in Transferable Development Rights (TDRs), Real Estate Business or construction of farm houses, manufacturing of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes of tobacco.
Single-brand product retail trading.
Civil aviation and non-scheduled air transport services.
Pharmaceuticals (Greenfield manufacturing).
ref: Rule 15 read with Schedule I of FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
explanation: FDI is strictly prohibited in: (a) Lottery business including government/private lottery, online lotteries; (b) Gambling and betting including casinos; (c) Chit funds; (d) Nidhi company; (e) Trading in TDRs; (f) Real Estate Business (excluding township/construction development); (g) Manufacturing of cigars/cigarettes; (h) Sectors not open to private investment (Atomic energy & Railway operations).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Land Border FDI Restrictions (Press Note 3 / Rule 6 Proviso)
question: Under the proviso to Rule 6 of the FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (reflecting Press Note 3 of 2020), an entity of a country which shares a land border with India can invest in Indian companies only under which route?
options: Only under the Government Approval Route, regardless of the sector or percentage of foreign holding.
Under 100% Automatic Route provided it is in technology manufacturing.
Under Automatic Route up to 49% and Government Route beyond 49%.
Investments from land-border countries are permanently barred.
ref: Proviso to Rule 6(a) of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
explanation: Under the proviso to Rule 6(a), an entity of a country which shares land border with India or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is situated in or is a citizen of any such country, can invest only under the Government approval route. Automatic route is completely unavailable.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) Rules 2022 - Financial Commitment Limit
question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, what is the maximum permissible limit of total financial commitment in all foreign entities by an Indian entity under the Automatic Route?
options: Up to 400% (four hundred percent) of the net worth of the Indian entity as per the last audited balance sheet, or USD 1 Billion per financial year, whichever is less.
Up to 100% of the net worth of the Indian entity.
Up to 200% of paid-up share capital exclusively.
Capped at USD 100 Million per project.
ref: Rule 13(1) and Schedule I of FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022
explanation: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, the total financial commitment made by an Indian entity in all foreign entities shall not exceed 400% of its net worth as per the last audited balance sheet, or as prescribed by RBI from time to time under the automatic route.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) - Framework & Minimum Maturity
question: Under the Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) issued by the Reserve Bank of India, what is the Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) for foreign currency denominated ECBs raised up to USD 750 Million per financial year under the Automatic Route for general corporate purposes?
options: Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) of 5 years (or 3 years for eligible manufacturing sector companies).
MAMP of 1 year.
MAMP of 10 years without exception.
No maturity requirement if interest is paid semi-annually.
ref: RBI Master Direction No. 5/2018-19 on External Commercial Borrowings (ECB Framework)
explanation: Under the RBI ECB framework, the Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) for general corporate / working capital purposes is 5 years. For specific manufacturing companies, it can be 3 years for borrowings up to USD 50 Million.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 13 - Penalties for Contravention of FEMA
question: If any person contravenes any provision of FEMA, 1999 or any rule, regulation, direction or order issued thereunder, what is the monetary penalty leviable under Section 13(1) where the amount involved is quantifiable?
options: Up to thrice (3 times) the sum involved in such contravention, and where the amount is not quantifiable, up to ₹2 Lakhs, and for continuing contravention a further penalty up to ₹5,000 per day.
Fixed penalty equal to 100% of the transaction amount.
Imprisonment for 7 years without option of monetary penalty.
A penalty up to ₹10 Lakhs strictly.
ref: Section 13(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 13(1), if any person contravenes any provision of this Act, or any rule, regulation, notification, direction or order, he shall be liable to a penalty up to thrice the sum involved in such contravention where the amount is quantifiable, or up to two lakh rupees where the amount is not quantifiable, and where such contravention is a continuing one, further penalty which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day after the first day.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15 - Compounding of Contraventions
question: Under Section 15 of FEMA, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2000, which of the following contraventions CANNOT be compounded by the Reserve Bank of India?
options: A contravention where a similar contravention committed by the person was compounded within a period of three years from the date of the present contravention, or contraventions involving serious money laundering/hawala angles.
Failure to file Advance Reporting Form within 30 days of receiving inward remittance.
Delay in filing Form FC-GPR beyond 30 days of share allotment.
Borrowing ECB exceeding the prescribed all-in-cost ceiling.
ref: Section 15(1) proviso of FEMA, 1999 and Rule 4 of Compounding Proceedings Rules, 2000
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 15(1), where a contravention has been compounded, no further compounding of that contravention shall be done within a period of 3 years from the date on which that contravention was compounded. Any second contravention committed within 3 years must go to regular adjudication. Also, contraventions involving serious PMLA violations cannot be compounded by RBI.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Holding of Foreign Exchange by Resident Indian
question: Under Section 4 of FEMA, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange Management (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2015, what is the maximum amount of foreign currency notes/coins an individual resident in India can retain in cash for personal use?
options: Up to USD 2,000 (or its equivalent in foreign currency notes/coins) without opening an RFC(D) account.
Up to USD 10,000 in cash notes.
Zero cash retention; all foreign currency must be surrendered within 24 hours of landing in India.
Up to USD 50,000 provided it was received as a gift.
ref: Regulation 3 of FEM (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2015
explanation: Under Regulation 3 of FEM (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, a person resident in India is permitted to retain foreign currency notes, bank notes and foreign currency travellers' cheques exceeding not more than USD 2,000 or its equivalent in aggregate, provided they were acquired while on a visit abroad or from an authorized person for business travel.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 8 - Realisation and Repatriation of Foreign Exchange
question: An Indian exporter exports engineering goods worth USD 500,000 on January 1, 2024. Under Section 8 of FEMA read with Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, within what period must the full export value of goods be realized and repatriated to India?
options: Within 9 months from the date of export (or 15 months if goods are exported to an overseas warehouse).
Within 30 days from the date of shipment.
Within 180 days without any power of extension.
Within 2 years as per international trade terms.
ref: Regulation 9 of FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2016
explanation: Under Regulation 9, the amount representing the full value of goods, software or services exported shall be realised and repatriated to India within nine months from the date of export. For goods exported to an overseas warehouse, the period is 15 months from the date of shipment.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Acquisition of Immovable Property in India by PROI
question: Under the FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, can a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) or Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) acquire immovable property in India?
options: An NRI or OCI can acquire any immovable property in India other than agricultural land, farm house, or plantation property.
An NRI or OCI cannot acquire any property in India without prior approval of RBI.
An NRI can acquire agricultural land provided payment is made through NRE account.
An NRI can only lease property for a period not exceeding 3 years.
ref: Chapter IX read with Rule 24 of FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
explanation: Under Rule 24 of the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, an NRI or an OCI may acquire by way of purchase any immovable property in India other than agricultural land, farm house or plantation property, using funds received in India through normal banking channels by way of inward remittance or held in NRE/FCNR(B)/NRO account.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Acquisition of Immovable Property Outside India by PRII
question: Dr. Alok, a resident Indian doctor who was born and brought up in Delhi, wishes to purchase a residential flat in London for GBP 180,000. Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, how can Dr. Alok legally acquire this property?
options: He can acquire the residential property outside India using the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) within the overall limit of USD 250,000 per financial year.
He must obtain prior special approval from the Union Cabinet.
A person resident in India is completely barred from acquiring any immovable property outside India.
He can acquire the property only by taking a loan from a London local bank without remitting any money from India.
ref: Rule 21 of Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022
explanation: Under Rule 21(2) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, a person resident in India may acquire immovable property outside India by way of purchase out of the foreign exchange held in an RFC account or through remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) within the limit of USD 2,50,000 per financial year.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Authorised Person (AP) & Authorized Dealer Categories
question: Under Section 10 of FEMA, 1999, who empowers and issues licenses to Authorised Persons (including Authorized Dealers Category I, II, III and Full-Fledged Money Changers)?
options: The Reserve Bank of India, on an application made to it in this behalf, authorizes any person to deal in foreign exchange or in foreign securities as an authorized dealer, money changer or off-shore banking unit.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India.
The Ministry of External Affairs in consultation with Ministry of Finance.
The Indian Banks' Association (IBA).
ref: Section 10(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 10(1), the Reserve Bank may, on an application made to it in this behalf, authorize any person to be known as an authorized person to deal in foreign exchange or in foreign securities, as an authorized dealer, money changer or off-shore banking unit or in any other manner as it deems fit.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Export of Services & Softex Form Requirement
question: An IT services company in Bengaluru exports software code to a client in Germany via internet data transmission. What statutory compliance must the company perform under FEMA regulations?
options: File a SOFTEX form in triplicate with the designated STPI (Software Technology Parks of India) within 30 days from the date of invoice/certification.
File an EDF (Export Declaration Form) with the Commissioner of Customs.
Software exports via internet are exempt from all filings under FEMA.
Obtain an import-export license from the local municipal corporation.
ref: Regulation 6 of FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2016
explanation: Under Regulation 6(1) of FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, every exporter of software in physical or non-physical (satellite/internet) form shall submit a declaration in Form SOFTEX to the designated official of STPI or SEZ within 30 days of the date of invoice for certification.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Non-Resident Bank Accounts (NRE vs NRO vs FCNR(B))
question: Which of the following statements regarding Non-Resident External (NRE) accounts and Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts is ACCURATE under FEMA regulations?
options: NRE accounts are repatriable without limit and interest earned is exempt from Indian income-tax, whereas NRO accounts have a repatriation ceiling of USD 1 Million per financial year and interest is taxable.
NRO accounts allow unlimited tax-free repatriation while NRE accounts are completely non-repatriable.
Both NRE and NRO accounts can only be maintained in US Dollars.
NRE accounts can be credited with legitimate rupee earnings originating from within India without restriction.
ref: Schedule 1 and Schedule 3 of FEM (Deposit) Regulations, 2016
explanation: Under FEM (Deposit) Regulations, 2016: NRE accounts are maintained in Indian Rupees, principal and interest are freely repatriable without limit, and interest is exempt from income tax u/s 10(4)(ii). NRO accounts are maintained for domestic earnings; funds can be repatriated up to USD 1 Million per financial year upon payment of applicable taxes.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 37 - Directorate of Enforcement (ED) Powers
question: Under Section 37 of FEMA, 1999, who exercises powers of investigation in respect of contraventions under the Act?
options: The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) officers, who exercise powers conferred on Income-tax authorities under the Income-tax Act, 1961 with respect to search, seizure, summons and inspection.
The local State Police Station under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Central Vigilance Commission exclusively.
The Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under Companies Act.
ref: Section 37(1) and 37(3) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 37(1), the Director of Enforcement and other officers of Enforcement shall take up for investigation the contravention referred to in section 13. Under Section 37(3), the officers of the Directorate of Enforcement shall exercise the like powers which are conferred on income-tax authorities under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 3 - Dealing in Foreign Exchange Prohibition
question: Under Section 3 of FEMA, 1999, save as otherwise provided in this Act, rules or regulations, no person shall:
options: Deal in or transfer any foreign exchange or foreign security to any person not being an authorized person, or make any payment to or for credit of any person resident outside India in any manner.
Maintain a passport issued by the Government of India.
Buy goods manufactured outside India from a local supermarket.
Exchange currency at an authorized airport foreign exchange counter.
ref: Section 3(a) and 3(b) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 3, save as otherwise provided in this Act, rules or regulations, no person shall: (a) deal in or transfer any foreign exchange or foreign security to any person not being an authorized person; (b) make any payment to or for the credit of any person resident outside India in any manner; (c) receive payments on behalf of PROI without general/special permission of RBI.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 19 - Appeal to High Court under FEMA
question: Any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange may file an appeal to the High Court under Section 35 within what period, and on what grounds?
options: Within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision/order, on any question of law arising out of such order (extendable by High Court for a further period not exceeding 60 days).
Within 30 days on question of fact or law.
Within 90 days directly to the Supreme Court.
No appeal lies against the orders of the Appellate Tribunal under FEMA.
ref: Section 35 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
explanation: Under Section 35, any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the High Court within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision or order on any question of law arising out of such order. The High Court may condone delay for a further period not exceeding sixty days.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 3(3) - Cartels & Horizontal Anti-Competitive Agreements
question: Four leading cement manufacturers in western India enter into an informal unwritten understanding on WhatsApp to fix the ex-factory dispatch price of OPC 53 grade cement and collectively limit monthly production volumes to create artificial scarcity. Under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002, what presumption applies to such horizontal agreements?
options: Such agreement shall be presumed to have an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC), shifting the burden of proof onto the cement manufacturers to rebut the presumption.
The agreement is presumed legal unless the Competition Commission of India proves actual consumer loss in rupees.
Informal unwritten understandings cannot be treated as an agreement under Section 2(b).
Cartels are exempt from the Competition Act if cement is notified as an essential commodity.
ref: Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 3(3), any agreement entered into between enterprises or associations of enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade of goods or provision of services (horizontal agreements/cartels), which: (a) determines purchase or sale prices; (b) limits or controls production, supply, markets, technical development; (c) shares the market; or (d) results in bid rigging, shall be PRESUMED to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 3(4) - Vertical Agreements & Rule of Reason
question: A manufacturer of high-end sports cars requires all authorized dealers to sign a contract stipulating that dealers cannot sell cars below the minimum retail price prescribed by the manufacturer (Resale Price Maintenance) and cannot sell spare parts of competing brands (Exclusive Supply Agreement). How does the Competition Commission of India evaluate vertical agreements under Section 3(4)?
options: Under the 'Rule of Reason' test, assessing whether the agreement causes or is likely to cause an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) under the factors listed in Section 19(3).
Vertical agreements are per se illegal with strict statutory presumption of AAEC.
All dealership contracts are unconditionally valid under the freedom of contract principle.
CCI has no jurisdiction over vertical agreements between manufacturers and distributors.
ref: Section 3(4) read with Section 19(3) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Unlike horizontal agreements under Section 3(3) which carry a statutory presumption of AAEC, vertical agreements under Section 3(4) (such as tie-in arrangement, exclusive supply agreement, exclusive distribution agreement, refusal to deal, and resale price maintenance) are evaluated under the 'Rule of Reason' to determine if they cause or are likely to cause an AAEC under Section 19(3).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Abuse of Dominant Position & Predatory Pricing
question: Mega Telecom Ltd. holds a 68% market share in the relevant market for high-speed fiber internet services in Metro Zone. In order to drive out two newly launched regional competitors, Mega Telecom reduces its subscription price to ₹99 per month, which is far below its Average Variable Cost (AVC), while utilizing huge capital reserves. What specific abuse of dominant position does this constitute under Section 4?
options: Predatory Pricing under Section 4(2)(a)(ii) read with Explanation (b), being the sale of services at a price below cost with a view to reduce competition or eliminate competitors.
Fair promotional marketing permissible under consumer welfare schemes.
Legitimate price discrimination permitted under Section 4(2)(c).
An anti-competitive combination under Section 5.
ref: Section 4(2)(a)(ii) read with Explanation (b) of Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 4(2)(a)(ii), there is an abuse of dominant position if an enterprise directly or indirectly imposes unfair or discriminatory price in purchase or sale of goods or service, including predatory price. Under Explanation (b), 'predatory price' means the sale of goods or provision of services at a price below the cost, as determined by regulations, with a view to reduce competition or eliminate competitors.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 5 & 6 - Regulation of Combinations (Thresholds)
question: Under Section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as revised and amended), which of the following transactions constitutes a 'Combination' mandating prior approval of the Competition Commission of India (CCI) under Section 6?
options: Any acquisition, merger or amalgamation where the enterprise or group exceeds the prescribed statutory asset or turnover thresholds in India or abroad, OR where the Deal Value Threshold (DVT) exceeds ₹2,000 Crores and the target enterprise has substantial business operations in India.
Any merger where both companies are incorporated in the same State regardless of size.
Only mergers involving foreign multinational corporations with market share > 90%.
Any acquisition where payment is made in cash exceeding ₹100 Crores.
ref: Section 5 and Section 6 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
