explanation: Under Section 5 as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act 2023, a combination includes: (a) asset and turnover threshold criteria (individual enterprise or group); and (b) Deal Value Threshold (DVT), where the value of any transaction in connection with acquisition, merger or amalgamation exceeds ₹2,000 Crores and the enterprise has substantial business operations in India. Section 6 mandates prior notification to CCI.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6(2A) - Timeline for CCI Approval of Combinations
question: Under the amended Section 6(2A) of the Competition Act, 2002, what is the maximum statutory timeline within which the CCI must pass an order approving or rejecting a combination, failing which the combination shall be deemed to have been approved?
options: Within a period of 150 days (reduced from 210 days by the 2023 Amendment) from the date of filing notice.
Within 30 working days without any extension.
Within 365 days from the date of publishing public notice.
Within 60 days of hearing objections from third parties.
ref: Section 6(2A) of the Competition Act, 2002 (amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
explanation: Under the Competition (Amendment) Act 2023, Section 6(2A) reduced the outer timeline for CCI to form a prima facie opinion and pass an order on a combination from 210 days to 150 days (and prima facie opinion timeline reduced to 30 days). If CCI fails to pass an order within 150 days, the combination is deemed to have been approved.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 27 - Orders and Penalties for Cartels
question: Where the CCI finds that 5 tyre manufacturing companies formed a price-fixing cartel in contravention of Section 3, what is the maximum penalty the CCI can impose on each cartel member under Section 27(b)?
options: Up to three times of its profit for each year of the continuance of such agreement, OR ten per cent of its turnover for each year of the continuance of such agreement, whichever is higher (and now including global turnover).
Fixed penalty of ₹5 Crores on each company.
Penalties are restricted to 1% of domestic sales.
Compulsory confiscation of all factory machinery without monetary penalty.
ref: Section 27(b) proviso of the Competition Act, 2002 (amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
explanation: Under Section 27(b) proviso, in case of a cartel, the Commission may impose upon each producer, seller, distributor, trader or service provider included in that cartel, a penalty of up to three times of its profit for each year of the continuance of such agreement or ten per cent of its turnover for each year of the continuance of such agreement, whichever is higher. The 2023 Amendment clarified that turnover includes global turnover derived from all products and services.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 46 - Lesser Penalty Regulations (Leniency Programme)
question: Alpha Glass Ltd., a member of a covert glass cartel, approaches the CCI and makes full, vital, and true disclosure about the existence, operations, and pricing formulas of the cartel before the Director General (DG) submits an investigation report. What benefit can Alpha Glass Ltd. receive under Section 46?
options: The Commission may grant up to 100% reduction in penalty to the first applicant who makes a vital disclosure enabling the Commission to form a prima facie opinion or establish the existence of the cartel.
Complete immunity from paying taxes to the Central Government.
A cash reward of ₹50 Lakhs from the Prime Minister's Relief Fund.
The leniency provisions apply only to non-corporate partnership firms.
ref: Section 46 of the Competition Act, 2002 read with CCI (Lesser Penalty) Regulations, 2024
explanation: Under Section 46 read with the Lesser Penalty Regulations, the CCI may grant up to 100% reduction in penalty to the first applicant who discloses the existence of a cartel before the DG report. Subsequent applicants can receive reductions up to 50% (second applicant) and up to 30% (third applicant) in order of their priority status, provided they offer continuous and complete co-operation.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53A & 53B - Appeals to NCLAT under Competition Act
question: Under the Competition Act, 2002, which appellate forum hears appeals against any direction, decision or order passed by the Competition Commission of India (CCI), and within what timeframe?
options: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), within 60 days from the date on which a copy of the direction, decision or order is received (with power to condone delay on sufficient cause).
The High Court of Delhi within 30 days.
The Supreme Court of India directly within 45 days.
The Securities Appellate Tribunal within 90 days.
ref: Section 53A and Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 53A, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) is the designated Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals against orders of the CCI. Under Section 53B(2), every appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date on which a copy of the direction, decision or order made by the Commission is received. Delay may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 48 - Offences and Contraventions by Companies
question: Where an enterprise contravenes any of the provisions of the Competition Act, 2002, who is deemed to be guilty of the contravention under Section 48?
options: Every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business, as well as the company, unless he proves that the contravention was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence.
Only the Company Secretary who signed the board minutes.
All equity shareholders in proportion to their shareholding.
Only the independent directors on the Audit Committee.
ref: Section 48(1) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 48(1), where a person committing contravention of any of the provisions of this Act or of any rule, regulation, direction or order is a company, every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the contravention and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 26 - Procedure for Inquiry on Complaints (Forming Prima Facie Opinion)
question: Under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, when an information is filed under Section 19 alleging contravention of Section 3 or 4, what action does the CCI take if it is of the opinion that there exists a prima facie case?
options: It shall direct the Director General (DG) to cause an investigation to be made into the matter.
It immediately passes a final cease-and-desist order without hearing.
It orders the immediate arrest of the Managing Director of the opposite party.
It transfers the matter to the local District Consumer Forum.
ref: Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 26(1), on receipt of an information or reference from the Central Government or a State Government or on its own knowledge, if the Commission is of the opinion that there exists a prima facie case, it shall direct the Director General to cause an investigation to be made into the matter. If no prima facie case exists, it closes the matter under Section 26(2).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 44 - Penalty for Making False Statement in Combinations
question: If an enterprise filing a notice of combination under Section 6(2) makes a statement which is false in any material particular or omits to state any material fact knowing it to be material, what penalty is leviable under Section 44?
options: A penalty which shall not be less than ₹50 Lakhs but which may extend to ₹5 Crores.
A penalty of ₹10,000 only.
Imprisonment for 14 years without bail.
Automatic confiscation of all assets of the acquirer.
ref: Section 44 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as amended)
explanation: Under Section 44, if any person, being a party to a combination, makes a statement which is false in any material particular, or knowing it to be false, or omits to state any material particular knowing it to be material, such person shall be liable to a penalty which shall not be less than fifty lakh rupees but which may extend to five crore rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 33 - Power to Issue Interim Orders
question: Under Section 33 of the Competition Act, 2002, does the Competition Commission of India have power to grant temporary injunctions (interim orders) restraining an enterprise from continuing an anti-competitive act?
options: Yes, where during an inquiry the Commission is satisfied that an act in contravention of Section 3(1) or Section 4(1) or Section 6 has been committed and that an order is necessary, it may by order temporarily restrain any party from carrying on such act until conclusion of inquiry.
No, only High Courts have jurisdiction to grant interim injunctions under Article 226.
Interim orders can only be granted in combinations, never in abuse of dominance.
Interim orders require previous sanction of the Attorney General of India.
ref: Section 33 of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 33, where during an inquiry the Commission is satisfied that an act in contravention of sub-section (1) of section 3 or sub-section (1) of section 4 or section 6 has been committed and continues to be committed or that such act is about to be committed, the Commission may, by order, temporarily restrain any party from carrying on such act until the conclusion of such inquiry or until further orders.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Settlements and Commitments (2023 Amendment)
question: Under Section 48A and 48B introduced by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, an enterprise against whom an inquiry is initiated for alleged anti-competitive vertical agreement (Sec 3(4)) or abuse of dominance (Sec 4) may apply for:
options: 'Commitments' before the DG submits the investigation report, OR 'Settlement' after the DG report but before final order of CCI, on payment of settlement amount and behavioral commitments.
Immediate closure of the case with zero financial payment.
Transfer of the case to an arbitration tribunal.
Settlement is available only for price-fixing cartels under Section 3(3).
ref: Sections 48A and 48B of the Competition Act, 2002 (Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
explanation: Sections 48A (Commitments) and 48B (Settlements) provide mechanisms for fast resolution. Commitments can be offered before DG submits report, while Settlements can be applied after DG report but before final order. Crucially, cartels under Section 3(3) are explicitly excluded from settlements and commitments.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 19(3) - Factors Determining AAEC
question: Under Section 19(3) of the Competition Act, 2002, which of the following is considered a pro-competitive factor evaluated by the Commission while determining whether an agreement causes an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC)?
options: Accrual of benefits to consumers, improvements in production or distribution of goods, and promotion of technical, scientific and economic development.
Creation of barriers to new entrants in the market.
Driving existing competitors out of the market.
Foreclosure of competition by hindering entry into the market.
ref: Section 19(3)(d), (e), (f) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 19(3), while clauses (a), (b), (c) are anti-competitive factors (creation of barriers, driving competitors out, foreclosure of competition), clauses (d), (e), and (f) are pro-competitive factors (accrual of benefits to consumers, improvements in production/distribution, promotion of technical/economic development).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 2(c) - Cartel Definition & Hub-and-Spoke Arrangements
question: An online platform algorithm facilitates parallel pricing across independent taxi fleet operators, where operators communicate through the common platform algorithm rather than directly with each other. Under Section 3(3) as amended in 2023, can the platform be held liable as part of a cartel?
options: Yes, under the amended Section 3(3) ('Hub-and-Spoke' cartel), an entity that participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of an agreement between horizontal competitors is deemed to be a party to the cartel.
No, because the platform operates on a different horizontal level and cannot be part of a horizontal cartel.
No, automated algorithms are immune from competition prosecution.
Liability arises only if the platform owns equity shares in each taxi operator.
ref: Section 3(3) proviso inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023
explanation: The Competition (Amendment) Act 2023 inserted a proviso to Section 3(3) bringing 'Hub-and-Spoke' arrangements into the statutory fold: an enterprise or person which is not engaged in identical or similar trade (like a platform or facilitator) shall be presumed to be part of the agreement if it actively participates in the furtherance of such agreement.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 2(t) - Relevant Product Market
question: Under Section 2(t) of the Competition Act, 2002, how is the 'Relevant Product Market' determined by the Competition Commission of India?
options: A market comprising all those products or services which are regarded as interchangeable or substitutable by the consumer, by reason of their characteristics, prices and intended use.
The entire territory of India where goods are transported.
Exclusively based on the GST classification code of the products.
The export market where foreign exchange is earned.
ref: Section 2(t) read with Section 19(7) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 2(t), 'relevant product market' means a market comprising all those products or services which are regarded as interchangeable or substitutable by the consumer, by reason of characteristics of the products or services, their prices and intended use. Factors under Sec 19(7) include physical characteristics, end-use, consumer preferences, and price classification.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 2(s) - Relevant Geographic Market
question: Under Section 2(s) read with Section 19(6) of the Competition Act, 2002, what constitutes the 'Relevant Geographic Market'?
options: A market comprising the area in which the conditions of competition for supply of goods or provision of services are distinctly homogeneous and can be distinguished from neighboring areas.
A market limited to the municipal boundary of a capital city.
Any region where state sales tax is uniform.
The entire continent of Asia.
ref: Section 2(s) read with Section 19(6) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 2(s), 'relevant geographic market' means a market comprising the area in which the conditions of competition for supply of goods or provision of services or demand of goods or services are distinctly homogeneous and can be distinguished from the conditions prevailing in the neighboring areas. Factors under Sec 19(6) include regulatory trade barriers, transport costs, and language.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 41 - Powers of Director General (DG) in Investigation
question: What powers are vested in the Director General (DG) of the CCI when carrying out an investigation into anti-competitive practices under Section 41(2)?
options: All the powers as are conferred on an inspecting officer under the Companies Act, including summoning witnesses, examining them on oath, requiring discovery and production of books, issuing commissions, and carrying out search and seizure operations.
Powers of a Chief Judicial Magistrate to pass criminal conviction orders.
The DG can only issue informal advisory letters without power to examine records.
Powers under the Armed Forces Special Powers Act.
ref: Section 41(2) and Section 41(3) of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 41(2), the Director General shall have all the powers as are conferred on the Commission under section 36(2) and the powers of an inspecting officer under the Companies Act. This includes summoning and enforcing attendance, examining on oath, requiring discovery of books, and carrying out search and seizure upon obtaining warrant from Chief Metropolitan Magistrate.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53N - Right to Claim Compensation Before NCLAT
question: A consumer group suffers financial injury of ₹12 Crores due to a price-fixing cartel penalised by the CCI. Under Section 53N of the Competition Act, 2002, how can the affected parties recover compensation?
options: By making an application to the Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) for an order for recovery of compensation from any enterprise for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered as a result of findings of the Commission or Appellate Tribunal.
By filing a civil suit before a Junior Civil Judge.
By approaching the Prime Minister's Grievance Cell.
No compensation can be awarded under competition jurisprudence.
ref: Section 53N of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 53N, the Central Government or a State Government or a local authority or any enterprise or any person may make an application to the Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) for an order for recovery of compensation from any enterprise for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered by them as a result of any contravention of the provisions of Chapter II having been committed by enterprise.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53T - Appeal to Supreme Court against NCLAT Order
question: Under Section 53T of the Competition Act, 2002, within what timeframe can an appeal be filed before the Supreme Court of India against any decision or order of the NCLAT?
options: Within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal (with power to condone delay for further period not exceeding 60 days).
Within 30 days without any extension.
Within 90 days from the date of filing of compensation claim.
No appeal lies against NCLAT orders.
ref: Section 53T of the Competition Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 53T, the Central Government or any State Government or the Commission or any statutory authority or any local authority or any enterprise or any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision or order on any question of law arising out of such order.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 124 & 125 - Contract of Indemnity vs Guarantee
question: Mr. Sharma enters into a contract with an insurance company promising to make good any loss suffered by the company due to an ongoing patent litigation by a rival firm. What is the fundamental statutory distinction between a contract of indemnity (Sec 124) and a contract of guarantee (Sec 126)?
options: A contract of indemnity involves two parties and primary liability arising on the happening of a contingency, whereas a contract of guarantee involves three parties (creditor, principal debtor, surety) with the surety's liability being secondary upon default of the principal debtor.
An indemnity requires three parties while a guarantee requires two parties.
A contract of guarantee must always be in writing while indemnity must be oral.
A surety in guarantee has no right of subrogation against the principal debtor.
ref: Section 124 and Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 124, a contract of indemnity is a contract whereby one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor or by any other person (2 parties, 1 contract, primary liability). Under Section 126, a contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default (3 parties, 3 contracts, secondary/collateral liability).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 128 - Surety's Co-extensive Liability
question: Bank of India grants a term loan of ₹50 Lakhs to Zen Infra Pvt. Ltd., secured by personal guarantee executed by Mr. Rakesh. Upon default by Zen Infra Pvt. Ltd., Bank of India files a recovery suit directly against guarantor Mr. Rakesh without first suing the principal debtor Zen Infra. Can Mr. Rakesh claim that the bank must exhaust its remedies against the principal debtor first?
options: No, under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless it is otherwise provided by the contract, enabling the creditor to proceed directly against the surety.
Yes, the creditor is legally bound to sell all assets of the principal debtor before touching the surety.
Yes, because a guarantor is only liable for 50% of the loan amount.
No, but the bank must obtain previous permission of the NCLT before suing a guarantor.
ref: Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad)
explanation: Under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. The creditor is not required to exhaust his remedies against the principal debtor before suing the surety (confirmed by Supreme Court in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 133 - Discharge of Surety by Variance in Terms
question: Mr. Verma stands surety to ABC Ltd. for the fidelity of Mr. Raman who is appointed as a cashier at a salary of ₹30,000 per month. Subsequently, without Mr. Verma's knowledge or consent, ABC Ltd. agrees to pay Raman on commission basis (which results in fluctuating income) and Raman is tasked with higher responsibilities. Raman misappropriates funds. Is Mr. Verma liable as surety under Section 133?
options: No, Mr. Verma is discharged as to transactions subsequent to the variance, because any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between principal debtor and creditor discharges the surety.
Yes, because the misappropriation occurred within the course of employment.
Yes, because variance in compensation does not affect the fidelity undertaking.
Mr. Verma is liable only to the extent of ₹30,000 per month.
ref: Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 133, any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. The change in Raman's remuneration and role without Verma's consent completely discharges the surety.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 140 & 141 - Surety's Right of Subrogation & Securities
question: Mr. Kishore stands surety for a bank loan of ₹20 Lakhs granted to Mr. Anuj. The bank also holds a mortgage over Anuj's commercial shop worth ₹15 Lakhs. Mr. Kishore pays the full ₹20 Lakhs to the bank on Anuj's default. What rights does Mr. Kishore have under Section 140 and Section 141?
options: Mr. Kishore is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor (Doctrine of Subrogation) and is entitled to the benefit of the mortgage over the shop, whether he knew of the security or not.
Mr. Kishore only has an unsecured personal claim against Anuj with no right over the mortgaged shop.
The mortgage over the shop gets extinguished automatically upon payment of debt.
The shop must be surrendered to the State Government.
ref: Section 140 and Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 140 (Right of Subrogation), where a guaranteed debt has become due and the surety pays all that he is liable for, he is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor. Under Section 141, a surety is entitled to the benefit of every security which the creditor has against the principal debtor, whether the surety knew of the existence of such security or not.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 148 & 151 - Bailment & Bailee's Duty of Care
question: Mr. Bajaj leaves his luxury car at a modern authorized service center for scheduled servicing. A flash fire breaks out in the adjacent paint booth due to defective electrical wiring installed by the service center without required safety circuit breakers. The car is completely destroyed. The service center points to a disclaimer printed on the job card: 'Goods parked and serviced at customer's own risk; management not liable for fire or theft.' What is the legal liability of the service center under Section 151 and 152?
options: The service center is liable for damages because under Section 151 the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed as a man of ordinary prudence would of his own goods, and a bailee cannot contract out of this minimum standard of care through an exemption clause where negligence is proved.
The disclaimer clause on the job card completely shields the service center from all liability.
The service center is only liable if the customer took out third-party fire insurance.
Under the Indian Contract Act, bailment does not apply to motor vehicle servicing.
ref: Section 151 and Section 152 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 151, in all cases of bailment the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed to him as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods. It is well settled that a bailee cannot contract out of the minimum statutory duty of care under Section 151 where damage is caused by his own negligence.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 170 & 171 - Particular Lien vs General Lien
question: Which of the following parties is entitled to a 'General Lien' under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, allowing them to retain any goods bailed to them as a security for a general balance of account in the absence of a contract to the contrary?
options: Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers.
Carpenters, tailors, and repairmen who have expended labor on specific goods.
All trade suppliers in wholesale commercial transactions.
Common carriers transporting agricultural produce.
ref: Section 170 and Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 171, bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, retain as a security for a general balance of account, any goods bailed to them. All other bailees (such as repairers, mechanics, tailors) have only a 'Particular Lien' under Section 170 in respect of goods on which they have expended labor/skill.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 172 & 176 - Contract of Pledge & Pawnee's Rights on Default
question: Mr. Kapoor pledges gold ornaments with a registered Non-Banking Financial Company (pawnee) as security for a loan of ₹5 Lakhs repayable in 6 months. Mr. Kapoor fails to repay on the due date. What legal remedies are available to the pawnee under Section 176?
options: The pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt and retain the goods as a collateral security; OR he may sell the thing pledged on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale.
The pawnee becomes the absolute owner of the gold ornaments automatically upon default without giving any notice.
The pawnee cannot sell the pledged goods under any circumstances without obtaining a decree from a civil court.
The pawnee must refund 50% of the gold ornaments to the borrower.
ref: Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 176, if the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt at the stipulated time, the pawnee may: (a) bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; OR (b) sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale. If proceeds are less than debt, pawnor is liable for balance; if surplus, pawnee pays surplus to pawnor.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 182 & 186 - Creation of Agency & Express/Implied Authority
question: A merchant in Kolkata employs an agent in Mumbai to purchase cotton. The agent purchases cotton on credit in his own name without disclosing that he is acting for a principal. Under Section 231 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what are the rights of the seller and the undisclosed principal?
options: If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other contracting party may refuse to fulfill the contract if he can show that he would not have entered into it with the principal; otherwise, the principal may require the performance of the contract, and the third party can sue either the agent or the principal.
The contract is completely void because agency requires disclosure of principal at the inception.
Only the agent is liable; the principal can never sue or be sued on undisclosed contracts.
The seller must file a criminal case for impersonation against the agent.
ref: Section 231 and Section 233 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 231, if an agent makes a contract with a person who neither knows, nor has reason to suspect, that he is an agent, his principal may require the performance of the contract. Under Section 233, in cases where the agent is personally liable, a person dealing with him may hold either him or his principal, or both of them, liable.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 201 & 202 - Agency Coupled with Interest (Irrevocable Agency)
question: Mr. Mohan borrows ₹10 Lakhs from Mr. Naresh and appoints Mr. Naresh as his attorney to collect rents from Mohan's commercial complex and adjust the collected rents against the outstanding loan until full repayment. Mohan subsequently issues a notice revoking the power of attorney. Can Mohan legally revoke this agency under Section 202?
options: No, where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest.
Yes, a principal has absolute right to revoke any power of attorney at any time.
Yes, provided Mohan pays a cancellation penalty of ₹50,000 to the sub-registrar.
The agency terminates automatically on the expiry of 1 year.
ref: Section 202 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 202 (Termination of agency where agent has an interest in subject-matter), where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest, nor does it terminate upon the death or insanity of the principal. This is an irrevocable agency.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 73 - Compensation for Loss or Damage Caused by Breach
question: A textile mill contracted to supply industrial fabric to a garment exporter by August 10. The mill failed to deliver. The exporter had entered into a lucrative export contract with a French buyer, which was cancelled, resulting in huge loss of extraordinary profits. The exporter had not informed the mill about the French contract at the time of entering into the supply contract. Can the exporter recover this special loss of profits under Section 73 (Hadley v. Baxendale rule)?
options: No, compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage; special damages can only be claimed if the special circumstances leading to such loss were brought to the knowledge of the mill at the time of making the contract.
Yes, all losses whether direct, indirect, remote or speculative are recoverable upon breach of commercial contracts.
Yes, but only if the exporter obtains a certificate of damages from a Chartered Accountant.
The exporter can recover 50% of the French contract profits under the rule of equity.
ref: Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Hadley v. Baxendale)
explanation: Under Section 73, compensation is payable for loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Compensation is not payable for remote and indirect losses. Special damages for loss of the French contract cannot be recovered because the special circumstances were never communicated to the supplier.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 74 - Liquidated Damages vs Penalty
question: A software development contract specifies that in case of any delay beyond December 31, the developer shall pay liquidated damages of ₹10,000 per day of delay. The developer delays completion by 20 days. Under Section 74, what amount is the aggrieved client entitled to receive from the Court?
options: Reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount of ₹10,000 per day (the stipulated amount), whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby.
The entire contract price becomes forfeited automatically.
Double the stipulated amount as punitive damages.
Zero compensation unless the client proves actual cash losses with bank receipts.
ref: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass / Maula Bux)
explanation: Under Section 74, when a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 68 to 72 - Quasi-Contracts & Unjust Enrichment
question: A delivery agent mistakenly delivers a consignment of expensive imported dry fruits worth ₹25,000 to Mr. Rawat's residence instead of Mr. Rajput's residence. Mr. Rawat, knowing the goods were not intended for him, consumes the dry fruits with his family. What is Mr. Rawat's liability under Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
options: Mr. Rawat must repay or return the value of the dry fruits (₹25,000) under Section 72, as a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it.
Mr. Rawat has no liability because there was no offer and acceptance between the sender and him.
The delivery agent alone must bear the loss with zero liability on Mr. Rawat.
Mr. Rawat is entitled to keep the goods under the Law of Lost Property.
ref: Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 72 (Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion), a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it. Mr. Rawat is under a quasi-contractual obligation to pay for the consumed goods based on the doctrine of unjust enrichment.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 56 - Doctrine of Frustration & Impossibility of Performance
question: A music event management company leases an auditorium for a live international music concert on November 15. On November 10, an accidental earthquake completely destroys the auditorium building. What is the legal status of the contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
options: The contract becomes void under the Doctrine of Frustration (subsequent impossibility) because the performance has become physically impossible without fault of either party.
The event management company is entitled to sue the auditorium owner for damages for breach of contract.
The auditorium owner must build a new stadium within 48 hours.
The contract remains fully enforceable and rent must be paid in full.
ref: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Taylor v. Caldwell)
explanation: Under Section 56 (Doctrine of Frustration / Supervening Impossibility), a contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful (Taylor v. Caldwell principle).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 190 & 191 - Sub-Agent & Delegatus Non Potest Delegare
question: Under the legal maxim 'delegatus non potest delegare' embodied in Section 190 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when may an agent legally appoint a sub-agent to perform acts which he has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally?
options: Only if by the ordinary custom of trade a sub-agent may be employed, or from the nature of the agency a sub-agent must be employed, or with the express or implied consent of the principal.
An agent can delegate his duties to anyone at his sole discretion without exception.
A sub-agent can only be appointed if approved by a Notary Public.
Sub-agents are strictly prohibited under Indian law under all circumstances.
ref: Section 190 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 190, an agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts which he has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally, unless by the ordinary custom of trade a sub-agent may, or, from the nature of the agency, a sub-agent must, be employed, or the principal permits delegation.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 196 - Ratification of Unauthorized Acts
question: Mr. Deepak, without any authority from Mr. Pradeep, purchases 1,000 bags of wheat on credit on behalf of Pradeep. When Pradeep learns of the transaction, wheat prices have increased, and Pradeep ratifies the purchase. What is the legal effect of ratification under Section 196?
options: The ratification has the same effect as if the acts had been performed by his prior authority, making Pradeep directly liable to the seller from the date of the original contract.
Ratification creates liability only from the date of ratification, not retrospectively.
Unauthorized acts can never be ratified under the Indian Contract Act.
Deepak remains personally liable despite Pradeep's ratification.
ref: Section 196 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 196, where acts are done by one person on behalf of another, but without his knowledge or authority, he may elect to ratify or to disown such acts. If he ratifies them, the same effects will follow as if they had been performed by his authority (doctrine of relation back).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 134 - Discharge of Surety by Release of Principal Debtor
question: The creditor enters into a formal binding composition agreement with the principal debtor releasing the principal debtor from the debt upon receiving 40 paise in the rupee, without obtaining the consent of the surety. What is the effect on the surety under Section 134?
options: The surety is completely discharged by any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the principal debtor is released.
The surety remains liable for the remaining 60 paise in the rupee.
The surety's liability is converted into an independent promissory note.
The surety must pay the debt and cannot seek reimbursement.
ref: Section 134 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 134, the surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the principal debtor is released, or by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 139 - Discharge of Surety by Creditor's Impairing Remedy
question: A bank holds a loan guarantee from Mr. Goenka for a factory loan granted to Zenith Tubes. The bank also held hypothecation over machinery worth ₹30 Lakhs. Due to gross negligence of the bank manager, the factory gates were left unlocked and the hypothecated machinery was stolen. Is Mr. Goenka discharged as surety under Section 139 and 141?
options: Yes, Mr. Goenka is discharged to the extent of the value of the security (₹30 Lakhs) lost due to the creditor's act or omission impairing the surety's eventual remedy.
No, the surety remains 100% liable because the loss of security was caused by third-party thieves.
Mr. Goenka is discharged only if he filed a police FIR personally.
Creditors have no duty to preserve securities under guarantee law.
ref: Section 139 and Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 139, if the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety himself against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged. Under Section 141, if the creditor loses or parts with security without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of the value of the security.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 160 & 161 - Return of Goods Bailed & Bailee's Default
question: Under Section 161 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if by the default of the bailee the goods are not returned, delivered or tendered at the proper time, what is the bailee's responsibility for subsequent loss?
options: The bailee is responsible to the bailor for any loss, destruction or deterioration of the goods from that time, even if the loss occurs due to an act of God or accidental fire.
The bailee is only liable if the bailor sends a registered legal notice.
The bailee is completely exempt if goods are destroyed by fire without his active fault.
The risk of loss remains on the owner under all circumstances.
ref: Section 161 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 161, if, by the default of the bailee, the goods are not returned, delivered or tendered at the proper time, he is responsible to the bailor for any loss, destruction or deterioration of the goods from that time. Once the bailee fails to return goods on time, he becomes an insurer and is strictly liable even for accidental loss.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 238 - Effect of Fraud by Agent
question: An agent for a real estate firm, acting within the scope of his authority in selling flats, makes fraudulent misrepresentations regarding municipal sanctions to a buyer. What is the legal liability of the principal under Section 238?
options: The misrepresentations made by the agent have the same effect on the agreements made by such agent as if such misrepresentations had been made by the principal, rendering the contract voidable by the buyer and making the principal liable in damages.
The principal is exempt because fraud is an ultra vires act outside the scope of agency.
The buyer has no remedy against anyone under caveat emptor.
The contract remains fully binding on the buyer without any right of rescission.
ref: Section 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 238, misrepresentations made, or frauds committed, by agents acting in the course of their business for their principals, have the same effect on agreements made by such agents as if such misrepresentations or frauds had been made or committed by the principals.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 27 - Agreement in Restraint of Trade
question: Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is to that extent void. Which of the following is the sole statutory exception recognized under Section 27?
options: One who sells the goodwill of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer carries on a like business, provided such limits appear to the Court reasonable.
Non-compete clauses in employment contracts restraining employees from working for any competitor for 5 years after leaving employment.
Exclusive cartel agreements between competing manufacturers.
Agreements to fix prices across all retailers in a State.
ref: Section 27 Exception 1 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
explanation: Under Section 27 Exception 1, one who sells the goodwill of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill from him, carries on a like business therein, provided that such limits appear to the Court reasonable. Post-employment non-compete covenants are void under Indian law (Niranjan Shankar Golikari case).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 2(7) - Consumer Definition & Commercial Purpose Exclusion
question: Apex Heavy Machinery Pvt. Ltd. purchases an industrial generator costing ₹35 Lakhs for use in its automotive manufacturing plant. The generator breaks down repeatedly due to manufacturing defects. Apex Heavy Machinery files a complaint before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Can Apex Heavy Machinery maintain the complaint as a 'consumer'?
options: No, because under Section 2(7) of CPA 2019, a person who obtains goods for 'commercial purpose' is excluded from the definition of a consumer (unless purchased exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment).
Yes, any entity that pays consideration is unconditionally a consumer under CPA 2019.
Yes, provided the complaint is supported by a technical engineer's affidavit.
Companies are never permitted to file consumer complaints under any circumstances.
ref: Section 2(7)(i) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 2(7)(i) of CPA 2019, 'consumer' means any person who buys any goods for a consideration, but DOES NOT INCLUDE a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose. Under the Explanation, 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment. An industrial company purchasing machinery for manufacturing is excluded.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 - Pecuniary Jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions
question: Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021, what are the pecuniary jurisdictions of the District Commission, State Commission, and National Commission based on value of goods/services paid as consideration?
options: District Commission: Value up to ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission: Value exceeding ₹50 Lakhs up to ₹2 Crores; National Commission: Value exceeding ₹2 Crores.
District: up to ₹1 Crore; State: ₹1 Cr to ₹10 Cr; National: above ₹10 Cr.
District: up to ₹20 Lakhs; State: ₹20 Lakhs to ₹1 Cr; National: above ₹1 Cr.
District: up to ₹5 Lakhs; State: ₹5 Lakhs to ₹50 Lakhs; National: above ₹50 Lakhs.
ref: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commission) Rules, 2021 (Notification dated 30.12.2021)
explanation: By the 2021 Rules revising pecuniary jurisdiction under CPA 2019: District Commission entertains complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission where consideration exceeds ₹50 Lakhs but does not exceed ₹2 Crores; National Commission where consideration exceeds ₹2 Crores.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 82 to 87 - Product Liability
question: A consumer purchases a pressure cooker from an authorized retail shop. Due to a defect in the safety valve manufactured with substandard alloy, the cooker explodes, causing severe burn injuries to the consumer and property damage to the kitchen. Under Chapter VI (Product Liability) of CPA, 2019, who can be held liable in a product liability action?
options: A product liability action may be brought against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product under Section 82.
Only the retail shopkeeper who handed the box to the customer.
No product liability action can be initiated unless criminal charges of murder are framed.
Liability is limited strictly to the replacement of the pressure cooker with no damages for physical harm.
ref: Section 82, 84 and 86 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 82 of CPA 2019, a product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer or a product service provider or a product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product. Under Section 84, a product manufacturer is liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, or lacks adequate instructions/warnings.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 10 & 21 - CCPA Powers & Celebrity Endorsement Liability
question: Under Section 10 and 21 of CPA, 2019, what power does the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) possess regarding misleading advertisements and celebrity endorsers?
options: CCPA can direct withdrawal/modification of misleading ads, impose penalties up to ₹10 Lakhs (and up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent contravention) on manufacturers/endorsers, and prohibit an endorser from endorsing that product/service for up to 1 year (extendable up to 3 years).
CCPA can only issue non-binding recommendations to the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI).
Celebrity endorsers have absolute statutory immunity from prosecution.
CCPA can revoke the citizenship of celebrity endorsers.
ref: Section 21(1), 21(2) and 21(3) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 21 of CPA 2019, the CCPA may impose a penalty up to ₹10 Lakhs on a manufacturer or endorser for false/misleading advertisement (up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent violations), and prohibit the endorser of a false or misleading advertisement from making endorsement of any product or service for a period which may extend to one year (up to 3 years for subsequent violations). Endorser is exempt if he carried out due diligence.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 69 - Limitation Period for Filing Complaint
question: Under Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what is the limitation period within which a complaint must be filed before the District Commission, State Commission, or National Commission?
options: Within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen (condonable if sufficient cause is shown).
Within one year from the date of purchase of the product.
Within 90 days from the date of issuing notice to the seller.
Within 3 years as per the general Limitation Act, 1963.
ref: Section 69(1) and 69(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 69(1), the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Under Section 69(2), a complaint may be entertained after two years if the complainant satisfies the Commission that he had sufficient cause for not filing within period.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 41, 51 & 67 - Appeals & Pre-Deposit Requirement
question: An order is passed by the State Commission directing a builder to refund ₹80 Lakhs to a homebuyer. The builder intends to file an appeal before the National Commission under Section 51. What pre-deposit condition must the builder satisfy before the appeal can be entertained?
options: The builder must deposit fifty percent (50%) of the amount ordered by the State Commission before the National Commission can entertain the appeal.
Deposit of ₹25,000 only.
Deposit of 100% of the awarded amount plus interest.
Zero deposit is required for filing an appeal under CPA 2019.
ref: Second proviso to Section 51(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 51(1), no appeal by a person who is required to pay any amount in terms of an order of the State Commission shall be entertained by the National Commission unless the appellant has deposited fifty per cent (50%) of that amount in the prescribed manner. Similar 50% pre-deposit rules apply to appeals from District to State Commission (Sec 41) and from National Commission to Supreme Court (Sec 67).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 3 & 4 - Offence of Money Laundering & Punishment
question: Under Section 3 and 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party in any process connected with the proceeds of crime is guilty of money laundering. What is the statutory punishment prescribed under Section 4?
options: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 3 years but which may extend to 7 years (and up to 10 years if the scheduled offence is under the NDPS Act) and fine.
Simple imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to ₹1 Lakh.
Monetary fine only with zero prison sentence.
Detention in civil prison for 6 months.
ref: Section 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 4, any person who commits the offence of money-laundering shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine. Where the proceeds of crime involved relate to any offence specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule (NDPS Act), the imprisonment may extend to ten years.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 5 - Attachment of Property Involved in Money Laundering
question: Under Section 5(1) of PMLA, 2002, the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director may provisionally attach property involved in money laundering. What is the maximum validity period of such provisional attachment order before confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority?
options: For a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order.
For a period of 30 days only.
For 1 year automatically.
Indefinitely until completion of criminal trial.
ref: Section 5(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 5(1), where the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director has reason to believe that any person is in possession of proceeds of crime, he may by order in writing provisionally attach such property for a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order. The attachment must be confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 12 - Reporting Entities & Client Verification (KYC)
question: Under Section 12 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, every reporting entity (including banking companies, financial institutions, intermediaries, and designated professionals) must maintain records of all transactions for what minimum duration?
options: For a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity, and maintain records of identity of clients for five years after the business relationship has ended.
For a period of two years from the audit date.
For eight years under the Companies Act rules.
Records must be permanently preserved indefinitely.
ref: Section 12(1)(a) and Section 12(3) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 12(3) of PMLA, records of transactions referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) shall be maintained for a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity. Under Section 12(4), records of identity of clients and account files shall be maintained for a period of five years after the business relationship has ended or account closed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 24 - Burden of Proof in Money Laundering
question: Under Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, in any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime, upon whom does the burden of proof lie with respect to property being untainted?
options: In the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering, and the burden of proving that the property is untainted lies on the accused.
The prosecution (Enforcement Directorate) must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt without any statutory presumption.
The burden of proof shifts to the commercial bank where funds were deposited.
Burden of proof lies on the statutory auditor who certified the balance sheet.
ref: Section 24(a) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. UOI)
explanation: Under Section 24(a) of PMLA, 2002, in the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering. The burden of proof is reversed and placed on the accused to establish that the property is untainted (upheld by Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 35 - Manner in Which Complaint Shall be Made
question: Under Section 35(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided may be filed with a District Commission by:
options: The consumer, or any recognized consumer association, or one or more consumers having same interest (class action), or the Central Government, CCPA or State Government.
Only the individual consumer personally; associations cannot file complaints.
Only an advocate registered with the State Bar Council.
Only after obtaining a certificate of conciliation from the local police.
ref: Section 35(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 35(1), a complaint may be filed by: (a) the consumer to whom goods are sold or service provided; (b) any recognized consumer association; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest (class action); (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority (CCPA) or the State Government.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 34(2) - Place of Filing Complaint (Consumer Convenience)
question: Under Section 34(2) of CPA, 2019, can a complainant file a consumer complaint before the District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain?
options: Yes, CPA 2019 introduced an explicit provision allowing the complainant to file the complaint where the complainant resides or personally works for gain (in addition to where the opposite party resides or cause of action arises).
No, the complaint can only be filed where the registered office of the seller is situated.
No, the complaint must be filed in New Delhi before the National Commission.
Only if the seller gives written consent to the jurisdiction.
ref: Section 34(2)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 34(2)(d), a complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain. This is a major pro-consumer reform compared to the 1986 Act which required filing at the defendant's place.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Chapter V - Consumer Mediation Cells
question: Under Chapter V (Mediation) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, where does the Consumer Commission refer the parties for settlement if it appears that there exists elements of a settlement acceptable to the parties?
options: To the Consumer Mediation Cell established attached to the District, State or National Commission, with the written consent of both parties within 5 days.
To the local Gram Panchayat for customary arbitration.
To the High Court Lok Adalat compulsorily.
Mediation is prohibited in consumer disputes.
ref: Section 37(1) and Section 74 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 37(1), at the first hearing of the complaint after admission, or at any later stage, if it appears to the District Commission that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, it may direct the parties to give written consent within five days to refer the matter for settlement through mediation, and upon receiving consent, refer the matter to the Consumer Mediation Cell attached to that Commission.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 44 - Offences Triable by Special Courts
question: Under Section 44(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which court has exclusive jurisdiction to try an offence punishable under Section 4 of PMLA and any scheduled offence connected to it?
options: The Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed, designated by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.
The Court of Metropolitan Magistrate.
The National Company Law Tribunal.
The Armed Forces Tribunal.
ref: Section 43 and Section 44(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 43(1), the Central Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, designates one or more Courts of Session as Special Court(s). Under Section 44(1), an offence punishable under section 4 and any scheduled offence connected to the offence under that section shall be triable by the Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 45 - Twin Conditions for Bail (Strict Bail Norms)
question: Under Section 45(1) of PMLA, 2002 (as upheld by the Supreme Court), what 'twin conditions' must be satisfied before a person accused of an offence of money laundering can be released on bail?
options: The Public Prosecutor must be given an opportunity to oppose bail, and where the Public Prosecutor opposes, the Court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
The accused must deposit 100% of the disputed proceeds of crime in cash with the Enforcement Directorate.
The accused must surrender all foreign passports and promise to appear once a year.
Bail is an absolute right under PMLA and no special conditions apply.
ref: Section 45(1) of PMLA, 2002 read with Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (SC 2022)
explanation: Under Section 45(1) of PMLA, no person accused of an offence under this Act shall be released on bail unless: (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application; and (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 2(47) - Unfair Trade Practice Definition
question: Under Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which of the following practices is explicitly categorized as an 'Unfair Trade Practice'?
options: Refusal to issue a cash memo or bill for goods sold or services rendered, or disclosing a consumer's personal information without consent, or offering gifts or prizes without intention of providing them.
Offering genuine discounts during festive seasonal clearance sales.
Selling goods strictly at or below Maximum Retail Price (MRP).
Displaying bilingual ingredients list on food packages.
ref: Section 2(47)(vii), (viii), (ix) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 2(47) of CPA 2019, unfair trade practices include: not issuing a bill or cash memo (clause vii); refusing to take back defective goods or refund consideration within period stipulated in bill (clause viii); and disclosing to other persons any personal information given in confidence by the consumer unless made in accordance with law (clause ix).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 90 - Punishment for Manufacturing/Selling Adulterated Goods
question: Under Section 90(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, if a person manufactures for sale or stores, sells or distributes any adulterant or adulterated product which causes the death of a consumer, what punishment is prescribed?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 7 years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine which shall not be less than ₹10 Lakhs.
Simple imprisonment up to 6 months and fine of ₹20,000.
Warning letter and temporary sealing of shop for 3 days.
Mandatory community service for 100 hours.
ref: Section 90(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 90(1)(d), where the adulterant or adulterated product causes the death of a consumer, the person responsible shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 17 - Search and Seizure Authority
question: Under Section 17 of PMLA, 2002, who authorizes an authorized officer to enter and search any building, place, vessel, vehicle or aircraft and seize records and property involved in money laundering?
options: The Director or an officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorized by him, who on the basis of information in his possession has reason to believe (recorded in writing) that a person has committed an act of money laundering.
The President of the local Municipal Corporation.
A judicial magistrate through a bailable warrant.
The Registrar of Companies.
ref: Section 17(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 17(1), where the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by him for the purposes of this section, on the basis of information in his possession, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing) that any person has committed any act which constitutes money-laundering, or is in possession of any proceeds of crime, he may authorise any officer subordinate to him to enter, search and seize.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 71 & 72 - Enforcement of Orders & Penalties for Failure
question: If a person fails to comply with any order made by the District Commission, State Commission or National Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what punishment can the Commission impose under Section 72?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month, but which may extend to three years, or with fine, which shall not be less than ₹25,000, but which may extend to ₹1 Lakh, or with both.
Disqualification from voting in Lok Sabha elections.
Simple fine of ₹500 without imprisonment.
The Commission has no enforcement powers and must file a fresh suit in a Civil Court.
ref: Section 72(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 72(1), whoever fails to comply with any order made by the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month, but which may extend to three years, or with fine, which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (FEOA) - Key Threshold
question: Under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (related economic legislation), what is the minimum value threshold of economic offences specified in the Schedule for an individual to be declared a 'Fugitive Economic Offender'?
options: Total value involved in the economic offences or offences must be ₹100 Crores or more, and the individual has left India to avoid criminal prosecution or refuses to return to India to face prosecution.
Value of offence exceeds ₹10 Crores.
Value of offence exceeds ₹500 Crores.
Any bouncing of cheque under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
ref: Section 2(1)(f) of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018
explanation: Under Section 2(1)(f) of the FEOA, 2018, 'fugitive economic offender' means any individual against whom a warrant for arrest in relation to a scheduled offence has been issued by any Court in India, who: (i) has left India so as to avoid criminal prosecution; or (ii) being abroad, refuses to return to India to face criminal prosecution, AND the total value involved in such offence or offences is ₹100 Crores or more.
